Uniform Title: Saubhāgyataraṅgiṇī Author: Mukunda Manuscript: Part of NGMCP Manuscript No. 5-4656 Reel No.: A 175/11
Description: This is a liturgical manual (*paddhati*) for the worship of the goddess Tripurāsundarī, composed by a certain Mukunda. In it, he refers to the *Veda* and Vedic *yajña*.
With great reverence, he regards [this text] as a source for the teachings concerning the goddess Tripurā,
whom he identifies at the beginning of his work with the goddess Durgā of the *Devīmāhātmya*. Thus, he quotes here and there short passages from the Vedas and...

He quotes extensively from the Purāṇas. Notoriously, the Purāṇas draw freely from other sources, especially the Tantras. He cites from the *Kūrmapurāṇa* and the *Kālikā*, which are his favorites—particularly the latter—as well as the *Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa*, *Varāha*, *Viṣṇu*, *Bhaviṣya*, *Devī*, and *Matsya*.

Skanda, and Vāmana. The tantras from which he draws include the *Vāmakeśvara*, which he quotes most frequently; the *Jñānārṇava*; the *Tantrarāja*; the *Uttara* (likely the later redaction of the *Rudrayāmala*); and the *Durgātantra*, which suggests a relatively recent date. Other sources include...
*Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* and *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*. The text breaks off in the fifth chapter (*taraṅga*).

Saubhāgyataraṅgiṇī 1a).
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī.
Having prostrated before the power consisting of consciousness, the illustrious Tripurasundarī,
he composes for her [devotees] this *Śrīsaubhāgyataraṅgiṇī*.
Indeed, here all living beings desire happiness for themselves and wish that suffering not be theirs;

yet the attainment of happiness and the avoidance of suffering do not occur—nor does the ultimate cessation of suffering and abiding in bliss—without the knowledge of Brahman. For it is said: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself."
When that supreme weapon has been discharged, his karmas are exhausted;
knowing Brahman as bliss, he fears not even from the wicked.

"O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness. It was when you realized 'I am Brahman' that all this became [your very self]. For one who perceives this oneness, what sorrow can there be, what delusion? Having known the Self, one transcends sorrow"—from such scriptural passages as these, it is heard that the knowledge of Brahman does not arise without power (*śakti*) and devotion (*bhakti*).
Among the Purāṇas, she is praised and worshipped with flowers, incense, perfumes, and other offerings in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.

She bestows wealth, sons, and likewise auspicious wisdom regarding the Dharma. The connection is that she grants even that [wisdom] within oneself by which one thinks, "I am giving. Furthermore, when pleased, she bestows supernatural power (*ṛddhi*); being satisfied by offerings and the like, she becomes one who is to be served.

If another [deity] bestows supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and higher knowledge (*vijñāna*) equally according to the devotee’s desire; or rather, if she, being pleased by the accumulation of supreme magnanimity, bestows both—this is the meaning.
O Great King, go for refuge to that Supreme Goddess.
When propitiated, she alone bestows upon men worldly enjoyments, heaven, and liberation.
The particle *eva* serves to exclude connection with anything else. Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Therefore, one seeking liberation should take refuge in Pārvatī, the Supreme Goddess, who has become the self of all beings and whose nature is Śiva."
O King of kings, that reality which is pure by nature and auspicious cannot indeed be known without relying upon me; therefore, go to me for refuge.

Likewise, there is also a Śruti passage: "I myself declare this, which is favored by both gods and men. Whomever I desire, him I make pliant; whomever I dislike, him I make a Brahmin, a seer, and one of great wisdom. I bend the bow for Rudra, so that he may strike the hater of sacred knowledge with its arrow."
I bestow fame and tranquility upon the people; I have entered heaven and earth.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*: "She, who is separated from her own [husband] but endowed with the conduct of [proper] clothing and so forth, is auspicious; she should be accepted by the mantra-practitioner through the permission of the mantra. Without that, whatever one's own duty there may be—such as the propitiation of a deity and so forth—it would fall away, like a palace built of sand in a moment. Now, [an objection]:
It is heard in scripture that Śūdras lack the entitlement to recite mantras; as stated in the Mahākapila Pañcarātra:
"There is no mantra associated with the Veda that excludes the Praṇava.
Therefore, the Veda is the supreme mantra, and it is traditionally held that the Āgama is a portion derived from the Veda."
1b) Rites such as those for subjugation (*vaśya*) yield results that are either auspicious or inauspicious;
it is said that everything is accomplished through the Veda by means of faith, sacrifices, and so forth.
There are no sacrifices without the Veda, nor are there sacrifices devoid of the Veda;
therefore, the Veda is the supreme mantra, yet the mantra is not the Veda.
Śūdras have no entitlement to the mantras; for them, there is only the supreme discipline. Since they lack the nature of mantras, it is said that all ritual acts may be performed without mantras.
It is true that it has eight [senses] because of its nature as a horse and because of the context.
Or rather, this refers to the specific nature of these mantras.

As stated in the Meruyāmala regarding the temple-mantra: "For women and Śūdras, this mantra ending in *namaḥ* brings auspiciousness. Knowing this, Mahāsena may even initiate Caṇḍālas. Likewise, in the Yājñavalkya Saṃhitā:
A Śūdra and women should never recite Vedic mantras;
however, the wise desire that they may recite the Śiva-mantra ending in *namaḥ* or the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
The connection with the word "namontam" (ending in *namaḥ*) applies to both cases. In the *Devīyāmala*:
"If a twice-born man gives a mantra joined with the *svāhā* and the *praṇava* to a Śūdra, the Śūdra shall go to hell, and the Brāhmaṇa shall incur the status of a Śūdra."
Thus [it is said].

This may be so; nevertheless, there is no entitlement [to practice] without initiation (*dīkṣā*). As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Having entered the ritual initiation ending with the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and having heard the *tantra* obtained from the guru, one should [practice] the desired mantra."
Likewise.

For the twice-born who have not undergone initiation, there is no entitlement here to their own duties, such as Vedic study and the like; however, such entitlement arises following the initiation ceremony.

Likewise, those who have been initiated have no entitlement to the worship of the gods and other such rites performed with unrefined [grain]; therefore, one should make oneself consecrated by Śiva. Thus it is said.
And that [notion] is refuted; it would lead to the consequence of non-eternality.
"Prajāpati himself declared that for as many syllables as one imparts of mantras to a Śūdra, for that many times the sin of killing a Brahmin shall accrue."

This statement is true; for the prohibition against giving food remnants and so forth is intended for the superior *śūdras*, according to the reasoning already stated. However, there is no qualification for [such persons] regarding the hearing of the *Pañcarātra* and similar matters. As it is said in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"The *Pañcarātra* is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas."
In the *Kālikā Purāṇa* it is stated that for Śūdras and others, that [knowledge] does not ascend to the status of a Śūdra:
"Whether out of delusion or through desire, a Śūdra who recites a Purāṇa, a Saṃhitā, or a Smṛti, attains hell along with his ancestors, O destroyer of sin."
Likewise, in the Mahābhārata:
Whatever man should constantly hear this, or likewise should recite it,
he shall encounter nothing inauspicious, both in this world and in the next.
By the two Vedantas, one may become a Brahmin; a Kshatriya shall be victorious;
a Vaishya shall possess abundant wealth; and a Shudra shall attain happiness.
In this regard, the venerable teachers have stated: "A Śūdra shall attain happiness."
Not by hearing alone, nor indeed by the sacrifice of recitation; therefore, it is stated in the Śruti that a Śūdra does not attain [the fruit] through sacrifice.
"One should cause the four castes to hear" thus permits the hearing of the *Mahābhārata* and other such texts.
Furthermore, in the *Harivaṃśa*, it is said: "One born from a Śūdra womb is dear to the Sugati [heaven] through hearing.
The connection is with the distant [verb] "should hear" (*śṛṇuyāt*) and "should obtain" (*samavāpnuyāt*), which applies to the Śūdra;
whereas for those of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), the connection is with "should recite" (*kīrtayet*). Thus they say:
therefore, hymns and the like composed by ancient sages (*purāṇa-muni*) should not be recited. And in this way, for Śūdras and others...

The prohibition of a *mantra* applies by way of its connection [to the specific rite], because there is no definitive evidence [to the contrary]. Furthermore, it would follow that even ignorant persons could achieve victory in rites such as the *vṛṣotsarga* (the ritual release of a bull) through [the mere recitation of] the *rudra* hymns and so forth. Nor should it be argued that when another foot [of a verse] is joined, it becomes a different *mantra*, and thus the accomplishment of that particular effect is achieved; for Gautama states: "The *namaskāra* (salutation) is the *mantra* of this [rite]."

In the case of the Vedic and Tantric mantras prescribed for the three [classes], it is because of the injunction regarding the *namaḥ* mantra; for that alone generates the respective *apūrva* (unseen merit). Otherwise, the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of this world of moving and non-moving beings are differentiated by the qualities [of the deities];
the light of Āditya, Indra, and the others consists of mantras, and the all-pervading Lord is composed of them.
It is not described by being fixed upon colors such as white, red, or yellow;
it is not established specifically within the qualities (guṇas) nor within the elements (bhūtas).

Existing within, without, and indeed outside the bodies of embodied beings, she is the nature of self-awareness; she is to be pointed out by teachers through the indications shown to those who seek instruction.
Just as space is not perceived when it is attained by darkness,
so too [the *liṅga*] is equal for males and neuter beings, yet it is especially distinguished among women.
That which is called Pradhāna, that which is called the power of the Mother—
that which constantly pervades both you and me and yet remains withdrawn.
I am she, and you and others likewise; that [state] is known as non-duality (adveya). Within her, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded and brought to fruition.
"That [Śakti], however, is truly known by me alone as 'Being' through the nature of Time"—this is the statement of Śrī Nārāyaṇa addressed to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. Likewise, in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"That which is manifest yet indefinable, partless, and belonging to the Supreme Self..."
At that very moment, form becomes subtle, and the entire world is composed of me.
Having repeatedly accomplished this through the yoga of the eightfold reflection,
that reality which is made firm is the eternal nature of truth.
You are the supreme bliss, the very nature of the Supreme Self;
you are the power (*śakti*) of all beings and the purifier of all.
The Goddess, who is omnipresent, whose divine form is all-pervading, who possesses every form, and who is known as the Ancient One,
is always the liberator of Kṛṣṇa and others, as well as of all living beings everywhere, through her female forms. Thus it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*.
The entire universe, beginning with primordial matter (pradhāna), was created by you;
it rests within you, O Goddess, and dissolves into you alone; you indeed are the supreme goal.
Some call you alone the primordial nature (prakṛti), while others who know the Self call you the auspicious Śivā, the one beyond nature, in their refuge in Śiva.
In you reside Pradhāna and Puruṣa, Mahat, Brahmā, as well as Īśvara;
likewise, Avidyā, Niyati, Māyā, Kāla, and so forth, exist by the hundreds.
For you are that supreme power, infinite and most exalted;
you are entirely free from all distinctions, yet all distinctions are born from you as their source.
O Goddess, through you alone does one attain bliss;
you alone are supreme bliss, and you alone are the bestower of bliss.
You are the supreme apsarā, the highest ether, the great light, the stainless, the auspicious,
the omnipresent, the subtle, and the eternal Supreme Brahman.

*Prakṛti* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), according to the *Viśvaprakāśa* lexicon: "In its innate womb, *prakṛti* resides within the Supreme Self. She is the power of Śiva (*śivaśakti*). Regarding her own nature, he states: "She is indeed power (*śakti*) in the act of devouring [the world]. For, although she is the substratum of all distinctions and is established in the distinctions consisting of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), nevertheless—
She is her own, pure, and free from all differentiation, because differentiation is produced by qualities (*guṇa*); this is the intended meaning. And it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"I alone am the world; where there might be a second, let that be another [illusion]."
Behold these manifestations of mine entering into Maya alone, who is full of evil.
Likewise, in the Varāha Purāṇa:
Having spoken thus, that beautiful goddess, the supreme deity, then laughed; she said nothing further.
As she was laughing, he, bewildered, beheld the three worlds with all their moving and non-moving beings emerging from her body; in that very instant, he became absorbed within her mouth.
"By the messenger of Mahiṣāsura," as it is stated likewise in the Kālikā Purāṇa.
That by which the unmanifest, through the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas,
differentiates itself and makes itself manifest is called Viṣṇumāyā.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"The power of the Supreme Brahman is likewise this egg-like universe."

Also in the *Saṃketapaddhati*: "The entire universe is his power; the Great Lord is the possessor of power. Having thus described the union with power at the beginning of creation, he [Abhinavagupta] speaks of his own experience, saying "by you alone.
And it has been stated by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda as well:
And power does not desire separation from the nature of the possessor of power;
there is an eternal identity between these two, just as between fire and its capacity to burn.
Likewise.
Śiva is not devoid of Śakti, nor is Śakti devoid of Śiva;
both are joined together as one form, the supreme state of the Lord.
In the Vāmakeśvaratantra.
Devoid of Śakti, he is unable to do anything;
but when he is joined with Śakti, O Supreme Goddess, he becomes capable.
O Śivā, in the auspicious and subtle [reality], no name or abode exists;
nor, O Maheśānī, is there any pleasure whatsoever even through knowledge.

O Śiva, who bestows all auspiciousness, who is subtle and beyond the range of all the senses, difficult to know—[you are called] Vāma, Īśvara, Śiva, and so forth. "Dhāma" means light or knowledge; "śarma" means the form of ultimate bliss. [In you] there is no karma.
He says, "You alone," because even the happiness of others is dependent upon Śakti. Now, [one might ask]: "Is Śiva not distinct from the mind? [The answer follows: "No."
To this, he says: "You. And it is stated in the *Saṃketapaddhati*:
"Contraction is the Supreme Śakti; expansion is the Supreme Śiva.
Divided by the distinction between the signified and the signifier, and in the form of phonemes and principles (*tattvas*), [reality] exists as if contracted."

3a) It is called the power of Brahman (*brahmaśakti*). The very essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself, when oriented toward its effects, is designated by the word "power" (*śakti*); and this is the characteristic of those who possess true knowledge—that which transcends name, form, quality, genus, and defining marks, and is the supreme light.
That very state which has reached the ground is Śiva. Likewise, in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"In ultimate reality, some speak of a difference between power and the possessor of power;
however, yogins who are experts in the truth perceive their non-difference."
"Likewise, I grant you divine vision; behold my Supreme Lord.
Having said this much, he himself bestowed that knowledge upon Himavat.
He revealed his own divine form, that of the Supreme Lord—
a tranquil mass of light resembling ten million suns.
Abounding with thousands of garlands of flames, resembling hundreds of fires of cosmic destruction,
formidable with its fangs, difficult to behold, and adorned with a circle of matted locks.
Holding a supreme trident in his hand, he is of terrible form and fearsome, yet possesses a peaceful and gentle countenance; he is unsurpassed and full of infinite wonders.
Characterized by the parts of the moon, possessing a luster equal to ten million moons,
wearing a crown, holding a mace in his hand, and beautifully adorned with anklets.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents,
holding the conch and discus in his hands, desirable, three-eyed, and clothed in an animal skin.
Situated at the summit, or situated beyond the outer boundary, it is likewise both external and internal;
it is praised as consisting of all powers, possessing every form, and eternal.
That lotus which is worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and the lords of yogis,
has hands and feet everywhere, and heads and faces on all sides.
He beheld the Supreme Lord standing there, pervading everything.
And that king was not overcome by fear; rather, his mind was filled with joy.
Thus, the manifestation of the Lord’s form occurs in this very manner. Likewise, the Upaniṣad also says:
"Now, know that [Self] as being like Indra, like a madman, and like one intoxicated; what is this eye? "So be it," he said. Thereupon, it flowed forth from him.
He vanished right there in that very space, and a woman appeared—Umā Haimavatī, most resplendent.
He said to her, "What is this? She replied, "It is Brahman. He said, "In the victory of Brahman, you have indeed triumphed. Then he understood, "It is Brahman. Therefore, these gods...

Agni, Vāyu, and Indra surpass all other gods; for they do not touch what is left over as impure, and they were the first to know this [Brahman]. Therefore, Indra indeed surpasses all others, for he touches him most closely and was the first to know him.

The statement, "He knew [it] as Brahman," declares Śakra’s status as Brahman by describing his experience of the touch of Brahman; this is because the concealment of Brahman has been previously mentioned. And that power is none other than Śrī Mahātripurasundarī. As it is said in the Vāmakeśvara Tantra:
O Dear One, Tripurā is indeed the supreme primordial Śakti who has arisen;
through the division of the gross and the subtle, she is Mātṛkā, the source of the manifestation of the three worlds.
She, whose nature is that very [reality], has swallowed all principles without remainder;
once she has been fully realized, nothing else is admitted as superior.

The word *paramā* means most excellent; *hi* is used for emphasis, meaning "indeed Tripura alone. Because she is *ādyā*, that is, since she is the primordial *mātṛkā* from whom the three worlds arise, she is their progenitor.

The reason for this is that, through the division of gross and subtle, she alone has become the cause and effect in the manifestation of the born and the unborn. For she is the one whose nature consists of the entire collection of principles, such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the I-principle (ahaṃkāra), which were cast within her during the dissolution (pralaya). Now, it is heard in scripture that Brahman alone is the cause; to this he replies: "In her... [the rest of the sentence follows].

The meaning is this: when she has fully matured, having swallowed the entire universe without remainder and reached the state of expansion, there is nothing else that is "other" (para); rather, she herself is designated by the word "other" in that state.
As Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
"This Brahman, which is the self of all, is Tripurā, the Supreme Goddess.

Likewise, the Śruti also states: "The power of living beings is the primordial Tripurā-śakti," and so forth. Nor should it be suspected that these [scriptural passages] have any other purpose, because of their repetition and general consistency; and thus says the aphorism of the Great Sage (Vyāsa): [Abhyāsa-adhikaraṇa].
"Because of repetition [the Self within the *ānandamaya* is the Brahman]," and "because of the commonality of the goal. Likewise, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"O best of mountains, I am indeed to be attained through meditation, the yoga of action, devotion, and knowledge; not otherwise, even by ten million ritual acts."

"With devotion" means with single-minded intent. Likewise, in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*: "He becomes pleased after a long time through meditation, but after a short time through meditation and worship. Therefore, it is specifically worship that is being described.
[As stated] in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.
He who always worships or bows with devotion to Durāṃ is a yogi, he is a sage, he is wise; for him, liberation rests in the palm of his hand.
Even a heap of sinful karma as vast as Mount Meru or Mandara perishes by propitiating Caṇḍikā, like a malignant disease.
The hero, who constantly delights in the difficult forest [of spiritual practice], is never stained by the terrors arising from great sins, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.

The Śruti also states: "One should worship the Blessed Goddess with these mantras; then the Goddess reveals Her own self. Therefore, he who worships with these mantras is a Brāhmaṇa; he beholds the Lord and attains immortality. For this very reason, even chanting and other such acts partake in the status of being auxiliary limbs to this [worship]. Thus ends the work composed by the venerable Mukunda.
The first wave in the *Saubhāgyataraṅgiṇī* is completed.
Now, in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should contemplate the Supreme Guru;
and having contemplated Bhairavī, one should then rise and perform [one's duties].
Likewise, the cleaning of the teeth should be done with a mere measure of *maitra* [tooth-stick] that does not cause injury.

"One should then perform the morning bath. This is because Dakṣa has stated there that the connection with the Veda is intended for that time: "One should spend the Brāhma-muhūrta (the fourth watch) in the study of the Vedas; sleeping during the two watches [following] the last watch of the night (pradoṣa), one is fit for becoming Brahman."
For this very reason, Viṣṇu said: "The last watch of the night is called the Brāhma-muhūrta.
Regarding the meditation on the Guru, the Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā says:
O Goddess of gods, having risen in the morning, one should meditate upon a radiant lotus;
there, one should meditate on one's own Śrī Guru, who has the luster of camphor.
One should eternally worship you, who are perfectly serene, whose form is like a jewel, adorned with peace,
and whose hands are forever granting boons and fearlessness.
"From the statement in the *Jñānārṇava*: 'The lotus is at the aperture of Brahmā; at the aperture of Brahmā is one's own Guru.

And: 'For the pacification of inauspiciousness, one should meditate on [the channel] from the root to the aperture of Brahmā as a slender lotus-fiber, radiant like the rising sun. The term 'Bhairavī' is an elliptical designation (upalakṣaṇa) for the act of contemplating."
By the phrase "not even upon reaching the immediate [offense] from that," an intermediate ritual action is indicated in between; as it says in the *Vaihāyasa-pañcarātra*:
"Having divided the night into five parts, one should perform the worship of the deities and so forth during the remainder."
The practitioner should constantly perform recitation, fire-offerings, and likewise meditation.

Therefore, O Sovereign of the Lords of Consciousness in the three worlds, having received Your command, O Beautiful One, I shall rise at dawn and, for the sake of Your pleasure, follow the course of worldly existence solely by Your command. O Śrī Tripurā, Queen of the Gods, as I follow the course of worldly existence by Your command, may rivalry, contempt, strife, and negligence [be overcome].
"O Mother, let there be no fears for me; I know what is Dharma, yet I have no inclination toward it;

I know what is Adharma, yet I have no aversion to it. O Hṛṣīkeśī, dwelling within my heart, I do exactly as I am directed by you. Thus it is said in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā: "At the end of *klīm* is Kāmadeva, at the end of *sarva*..."
One should draw [the yantra] for the beloved within the heart; this mantra is for the purification of the teeth. Now, regarding the bath:
in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, it says, "Then one should perform the rite of bathing; one should sprinkle the body with the root mantra three times"—this is the remainder [of the instruction].
Then one should perform the rite of bathing while recollecting the root-vidyā;
having consecrated water three times in one's joined palms with the mantra, one should pour it upon the head.
One should cast [the water] away, according to the statement in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"With the syllables *Ātman*, *Vidyā*, and *Śiva*, one should perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) twice and three times;
and one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) three times, preceded by the gods, the sages, and the ancestors."

"By means of the Vidyā in three ways": having uttered the first *kūṭa*, [one says] "to the Ātmatattva, *tṛdhā*"; having uttered the second *kūṭa*, [one says] "to the Vidyātattva, *svadhā*. It is the same for the others as well. Thus, by means of the Vidyā which is threefold through the division of the three *kūṭas*.
"One should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana)," so it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*.

Having performed the sipping, one should then [sprinkle] the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, navel, and heart three times with mantras beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *svadhā*, starting from the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*).
One should touch the head; it is taught that the salutation of the ears and other limbs is performed with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
The principles (*tattva*) are considered to be Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, or alternatively, the Praṇava and the Vāgbhava-mantra.
Regarding the *vāgbhava* [syllable] within other mantras, he states that this is an alternative procedure (*anukalpa*) because of the specific injunction here, saying "it has been stated.
(4b) The connection is that one should perform the threefold libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the Vidyā, preceded by the gods, sages, and ancestors.
Having recited the mantra, [one says]: "I satiate Śrī Mahātripurasundarī."
Now, regarding the twilight worship (*sandhyā*): in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, it is said:
"Then the mantra-practitioner, adorned with all ornaments..."
With his body and garments red, and seated upon a red throne,
he performs the threefold consecration by means of the Vidyā whose nature is that of reality.
O Goddess, the wise one, having taken water into his cupped hands in three ways by means of the Vidyā alone, should contemplate that it has entered the flowing [currents], O Beloved.
O Dear One, the personification of evil stands in the left side of the belly, with the luster of lampblack;
his head is the murder of a Brahmin, and his two hands are the theft of gold.
O Supreme Goddess, the drinking of liquor constitutes the major sins (pātaka) in the heart and limbs, while the multitudes of minor sins (upapātaka) are the hairs on the body.
One should contemplate the multitudes of various sins as being all his limbs;
O Goddess, the wise man should contemplate him in his mind as bearing a sword and a shield.
O beautiful one, having visualized a vajra-stone upon the ground, one should strike there;
then one should offer the *argha* and recite the solar mantra three times.
O Goddess, Hṛllekhā is the heart; one should then utter Haṃsa as the head.
This Mahāvidyā of four syllables is the supreme deity of all the gods.
She wears a crown of shimmering clusters of radiant jewels and bears the crescent moon;
she possesses the luster of freshly smelted gold and has the form of the solar disc.

Then, meditating on her holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting, the practitioner of mantra should recite the auspicious Gāyatrī three times, which consists of the nature of the seed-syllables.
O Goddess, one should write "vāk" at the end of the well; then "vāgīśvari ca vidmahe.
Having uttered the second *kūṭa*, one writes "kāmeśvari ca dhīmahi."
Having uttered the third peak-syllable (*kūṭa*), one should cause the Power (*śakti*) to impel it therein;
one should perform the recitation according to one's capacity, and thereafter recite the Śrīvidyā.

The connection is that one should perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) with the *vidyā* consisting of the three principles (*tritattva*), which possesses the nature of the three [mantras]. Having taken water in the hollowed palms (*culuka*), one should perform the sprinkling (*mārjana*)—that is, the triple consecration (*abhiṣecana*)—with the *vidyā*; this is the implied meaning.
This has been stated in the Śaiva Āgama:
Taking water from the left hand with the right hand,
sprinkling it over the head in sequence with the mantras is declared to be *mārjana*.
"Having led it to the vicinity of the nose, [the practitioner] should hold it within the hollow of the right hand"—by the word "wise" (sudhīḥ), this is indicated:

one should contemplate that the personification of sin (pāpapuruṣa), which was flowing in the water of the cupped hands, has entered through the nostril. Hṛllekhā is the heart; *hrāṃ* is her head; *hasaḥ* is her seed-syllable (*bīja*). There is an option regarding its use together with the root-mantra (*mūla*).

"Or, O Goddess, with the root-mantra, or with the Sūrya-mantra, O Beloved"—thus from the statement in the *Jñānārṇava*. The word "kūṭa" refers to the *vālā* [the *māyā-bīja*], because the word "bīja" was mentioned at the beginning; for in various sections of the *Jñānārṇava*, having extracted the Gāyatrī joined with that seed-syllable and having described bathing and other rites, [it speaks of] Sundarī.
In this context, O Goddess of gods, having risen at dawn and bowed to the Guru by his own names,

one should perform the morning twilight rites, bathing, and so forth, O Goddess, with the understanding that the mantra is [the name] itself; for there is no mention of entering [the mandala] otherwise.
Because it refers to that which was previously mentioned:
*Aiṃ vāgīśvari vidmahe klīṃ kāmeśvari dhīmahi | sauḥ tannaḥ śaktiḥ pracodayāt*—this is the Gāyatrī. At dawn it is Sāvitrī; at midday it is Sarasvatī.
And because it is designated as "evening" in the *Tripuropaniṣad*: "In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, by reciting the root mantra, one reaches home unharmed;
having reached it, one should diligently wash both hands and feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*)."

"Having reached the sacrificial pavilion, one should enter after performing a circumambulation"—thus it is said; and regarding the statement "one should then recite the Śrīvidyā," he explains it himself:
"Now, the auspicious sacrificial hall, adorned with lac..."
On the ground, which has been smeared with cow dung, one should place many beautiful flowers.
Seated there was [the deity], beautiful with radiant flowers, adorned with incense,
charming with rows of lamps, and brilliant with scattered blossoms.
Having arrived there, the wise man—silent, learned, and always pure—should perform the sacrifice.
Likewise, in the Vāmakeśvaratantra:
His body was reddish-brown like saffron, adorned with red garments;
his mouth was filled with betel-leaf, and he was fragrant with the scent of incense.
His body is smeared with camphor powder, adorned with red ornaments,
covered with red flowers, observing silence, and anointed with red perfumes.
Seated upon a red seat, situated within a house as crimson as lac,
he is known for his attire of complete adornment, his body formed into three cities.
Or the practitioner, whose mind is steady and who is devoted to mental resolve,
[should practice] on a level, pure plot of ground smeared with cow dung.
O Goddess, [it should be] strewn with heaps of flowers, fragrant and perfumed with incense,
and further [adorned] with vermilion powder or saffron.
One should first draw a beautiful wheel, perfectly symmetrical,
with three equal triangles and a tip shaped like a spear (śakti), accompanied by its consort, and exceedingly lovely.
O Goddess, having meditated upon the three cities accompanied by the three seed-syllables, [anoint it] with yellow pigment,
camphor, saffron, and light musk.
O Goddess, one should perform the purification of the hands with the *sarvādya-vidyā*;
thereafter, O Īśvarī, one should offer the seat of the self (*ātmāsana*) and then the seat of the wheel (*cakrāsana*).
O Goddess, the seat of all mantras is likewise equal to the *sādhya* and *siddha* [states];
thereafter, one should perform protection by means of the previously mentioned *kula-vidyā*.
By means of the yoga of the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) accompanied by salutation,
[one should place them] on the head, the forehead, between the eyebrows, the throat, the heart, and the region of the navel.
One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) with eight [syllables] upon the support (*ādhāra*) up to the emanation (*vyūhaka*).

This means having a mouth filled with the red dye of betel; for it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*: "With a face possessing the hue of betel and a mind delighted by passion (*madana*)," and it is also mentioned in the *Ṣaṭsahasrī*: "With a lower lip reddened by betel."
"Adorned with all types of horn-axes and the like, having made himself amorous with ointments and so forth, wearing the guise of a lamp,
bearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on his body, and his eyes colored with collyrium"— thus it is stated in that very same [text]. 5b)

"Having made his body tripurīkṛta" means having adorned it with red sandalwood and so forth by means of the placement (nyāsa) to be described hereafter, according to the statement in the *Śrīkrama*: "adorned with red sandalwood. "Steady-minded" means one whose mind is one-pointed. The term "region of the earth" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa).
Alternatively, having fashioned a cloth-strip from gold or silver, or from copper, or from various metals,
using sandalwood or red sandalwood;
Having placed it upon a cloth, one should write it with a pen made of gold, O beloved.
According to the statement in the *Jñānārṇava*: "With *rocanā* and *kuṅkuma*, as well as with *kastūrī*, *candana*,
and *indubhi*," the wise man should draw [the diagram] on a stone from the banks of the Gaṇḍakī, on gold, silver, or copper, on *kāśmīra*, on a mirror, or on birch bark, upon a beautiful seat.
And from the words of Dakṣiṇāmūrti: "Manorama" means that which gladdens the mind.
"Samāstrikoṇa" refers to a triangle with equal sides, wherein the power (śakti) resides. The method for drawing this is described in the Jñānārṇava:
"One should draw a straight line from Īśāna to Agni."
The preceptor, drawing two lines from the northeast toward the southeast, starting from the tip of the fire-altar;
O Dear One, having unified [the elements] with the Vāruṇī, one should draw the supreme Śakti-rekhā above it in the form of a triangle.
The form shaped like a triangle is said to consist of two powers;
one should draw the excellent measuring-staff (mānayaṣṭi) in the portion belonging to the eastern power.
O Supreme Goddess, one should then [draw] a line from the northwest corner to the southwest corner;
by means of the sequence of dividing the joints, thereafter follows the power of those two.
Having drawn lines from the two corners, perform the rising [of the lines] as before;
this is the fire-maṇḍala with its tip pointing east, O Goddess worshipped by heroes.
And at the end, that triad came to be; listen to this, O fair-faced one, from the two corners in the east, [formed] by Śaktīśa and Vahni, O goddess worshipped by the gods.
Having extended the eastern line,
one should likewise draw a western line from the southeast toward the northwest and southwest corners.
Having expanded it, O Goddess, one should join it according to the sequence of the division of the joints:
[placing] that which goes to the tip of the womb in the eastern region, proceeding in order from south to north.
Likewise, when the lines are similarly arranged in the western direction in sequence,
by joining them to the tips of the corners, it then becomes a ten-cornered figure.
In the same way, O Goddess of the gods, there is a second ten-cornered [figure],
with lines from the northeast to the southeast and from the eastern womb-tip in reverse order.
Having expanded it, one should subsequently join it in the western direction in due order;
having expanded the lines at the tips of the wind and rakshasa corners as before.
Then, O Goddess, one should join the western end with that which lies in the direction of Indra (the east);
it is beautiful when the two ends are brought together at a single point in the eastern corner.
O Goddess of the gods, one should join [the lines] so that it becomes a pentagon;
O Goddess of the gods, having omitted four corners of the ten-cornered [figure].
O Goddess, one should draw the central lines between the two ends of the ten corners:
two in the southern division and likewise in the northern division.
Then, O Goddess, by means of the sequential breaking of the joints of the hexagon,
having joined the Yoni and Vahni, the letter Śakra (Ś) is then produced.
One should join the lines situated in each successive section so that they take a straight form,
O Goddess, so that it becomes beautiful and pleasing to the mind.
O fair-faced one, this wheel consists of five spokes facing forward, four fire-points at the front,
and a bindu within a triangle.
Know, O Goddess, that the middle wheel likewise consists of two sets of ten spokes;
it is marked with the *śakrayoni* (thunderbolt-womb) and is situated between the outer and inner [circles].
O Great Goddess, this wheel increases all good fortune;
O Goddess, it bestows universal sovereignty and destroys the bonds of all calamities.
O Goddess, it is filled with many horses, rubies, and gold;
it bestows great liberation and brings about the great play of speech.
O Maheśānī, this circle outside, resembling the full moon, should be joined with eight petals,
O Mīnākṣī, making it captivating.
Then, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should draw a sixteen-petaled [lotus],
O Supreme Lady, together with a square and four gates.
O one of great splendor, since sixty-four million yoginīs enter into this wheel,
they indeed honor the practitioner.
A square mandala adorned with the letters of the Mātṛkā for the sake of attaining siddhi,
resplendent with a level ground set with pearls and rubies.
Named Trailokyamohana, it bestows the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree;
it has sixteen spokes, takes the form of the lunar orb, and is the abode of its own digits.
O auspicious one, it fulfills all hopes and showers the nectar of sentient beings;
O Great Goddess, it has eight petals and resembles the color of the hibiscus flower.
That which is named "Agitator of All," and that which "Sets in Motion All Desires"—
these three, O lady of excellent hips, constitute the Wheel of Emanation (sṛṣṭicakra) that bestows happiness.
O Goddess of the gods, the fourteen-spoked [cakra], adorned by the supreme goddess of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya), bestows all siddhis and has the luster of a pomegranate flower.
O auspicious one, it bestows infinite fruit and always grants all prosperity;
O beloved, it has ten spokes, shines like molten gold, and resembles vermilion.
The wheel that accomplishes all aims always bestows the mind and consciousness;
the second [wheel] also has five spokes and resembles the hibiscus flower.
O Śivā, this wheel which produces all protection consists of great wisdom;
O Great Goddess, these three constitute my wheel of persistence, which bestows happiness.
O lady of excellent hips, it is adorned by the Goddess of the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya), bestows all perfections,
is eight-cornered, and is as red as the rays of the rising sun.
Resembling a ruby in appearance, it always removes all diseases;
it possesses the brilliance of a thousand rising suns and the luster of the bandhūka flower.
The wheel that bestows all accomplishments, the abode of all things, the Lord,
the triangle which is the cause of all manifestation and the eternal granter of prosperity.
O lady of excellent hips, the Bindu-cakra is supreme, consisting of all-bliss;
O Supreme Goddess, it is the leader of the cakras, composed of Sadāśiva.
This wheel is the eternal support, its form always consisting of Brahman;
it is to be served according to the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), and its triad is worshipped in the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya).
O Goddess praised by heroes, the six paths exist within this wheel; O Mistress of the Gods praised by heroes, when the six paths are present upon the petals of the wheel.
O sinless one, I shall explain: within the three junctions of the *pattra*, the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) is established; the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) has the form of the *mātṛkā*.
6b) O Dear One, since the eight groups of the Mātṛkā are established in the directions,
know that the sixteen-spoked [mandala] consists of the earth-element and is composed of those [groups], which are the essence of the Kalās.
The eight petals are marked with the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*, arranged in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
the letters from *ka* to *ḍha*, which are the letters of Indra, are situated in the corners of Indra.
The ten syllables beginning with *ṇa* and ending with *bha* are in the first ten-spoked wheel;
those beginning with *ma* and ending with *kṣa* are in the second ten-spoked wheel as well.
I shall now describe the eightfold armor within the eight corners and the triangle:
beginning with 'A' and ending with the three lines, the pair 'Ha-Kṣa' is situated in the center.
O Goddess, the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) has been described as the Mātṛkā in the form of the sacred seats (pīṭha);
the wheel (cakra), consisting of the thirty-six principles (tattva), arises according to its fundamental nature.
Bound by five lion-thrones, she who eclipses the arts through her command of the wheel is that Mahātripurasundarī, joined with Bālā Bhairavī.
O sinless one, it is certain that the mantra always expands, pervading the wheel beginning with Tripura and ending with Ambikā; this is known as the Dhvaja-mantra.
In this way, one should contemplate the pure Śrīcakra within the six pathways (ṣaḍadhvan).
However, worship on bare ground is prohibited, as it has been stated by Īśānaśiva:

In the same way, one should worship Śakti as one with oneself in a mandala, on a painting, or on a cloth; or one may worship this Great Bliss (Māhāda) situated upon a sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila). The masters of mantra declare that otherwise, one shall fall away from the three aims of life (trivarga).
"The three cities" refers to that which consists of the principles of Ātman, Vidya, and Śiva; which is composed of the orbs of the Moon, Sun, and Fire;
which is composed of Will, Knowledge, and Action; or which is composed of the triad of powers (śakti) in the form of Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī.
The "three seed-syllables" are those connected with the Root-Vidyā. As stated in the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*:
Having written a vast and brilliantly radiant wheel with vermilion,
the practitioner should constantly worship it, endowed with the fifty syllables.
The phrase "having uttered the mantra" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

According to the statement in the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*: "O Goddess, with the primordial Vidyā, which is the Bālā [consisting of] three peaks, one should perform the purification of the hands; with that very same Vidyā, the practitioner should effect protection for himself. Thus, one should perform the purification of the hands and protection by means of the Bālā-vidyā.

The statement from the *Vāmakeśvara* [Tantra] should also be interpreted in accordance with this very principle. Alternatively, she consists of the seed-syllables beginning with the Bindu and the two vowels, as stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Having uttered the first, which is Vāgbhava, and the second, which is the Kāma-bīja..."
But for the maiden, the third is indeed the supreme goddess Tripurā.
The first supreme goddess is the Vidyā that effects the purification of the hands;
one should perform the purification of the hands with this Vidyā, beginning from the middle fingers and ending at the palms.
Repeating this twice over the fingers is considered the purification of the hands.

The word "should place" (*nyaset*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. "From the middle" refers to the order of maintenance (*sthiti-krama*). As it is stated in the *Vāyavīya-saṃhitā*:
"One should place [the letters] starting from the middle and ending with the final letter (*niṣṭhā*); this is the order of maintenance.
He states another method of placement (*nyāsa*) with the word "then" (*tataḥ*), meaning "one should give," i.e., one should place. As it is stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā*:
Having performed the ritual purification of the hands, one should place the deities of the four seats upon the feet, the calves, the knees, and the mūlādhāra.

7a) One should place the mantras— whether with flowers, with water, or even mentally— upon the deities, as described in the *Jñānārṇava*. Having omitted the first mantra of Tripura, one should surround Bhuvaneśī [with the others].
"One should offer the seat of the Self with this [mantra]," it is said.
O Maheśānī, when Tripureśī abides within the three seed-syllables,
know her, O Goddess, as Tripurasundarī, who has entered the seat of the cakras.
Likewise, in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā, it is said:
"This triad of seeds, beginning with the seed of Śiva, has been proclaimed."

Regarding the term *tripureśyā*: in the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*, however, it is said: "In the same way, O Maheśvarī, the seed-syllable of Soma (sa) is joined with the vowel 'e' (ekārānta); when joined with the foremost vowel of the seed-syllables, it becomes the *kūṭa* of Śakti."
"With these, one should offer the wheel-throne (*cakrāsana*). The seed-syllable of Soma is the letter *sa*; the vowelless [syllable] is the letter *ha*. Likewise, in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Mistress of Tripura, O Great Goddess, in the *vāgbhava* and the *kāmarāja* [kūṭas]," [it continues].
She whose form is Śiva is joined with the third [vowel] conjoined with the moon of Śiva.
This Śrī Tripurā is considered to have resorted to the seat of all mantras;
however, O Daughter of the Mountain, when she has resorted to the seat of the Self, one should omit the third [syllable].
Having superimposed the essence of power (*vala*), she is seated upon the throne of the accomplished goal (*sādhyasiddhāsana*).

The essence of power consists of the three syllables beginning with *va* joined together; it is conjoined with the letter *va*, linked to the letter *śa*, and endowed with the eleventh vowel (*au*). Crowned by the bindu at its head, this is the great throne of the accomplished goal—thus says the *Śrīkrama*.

Because of the statement: "From that," the connection is that one should perform protection by means of the family lore (*kulavidyā*) joined with the *namaskāra*, through the application of the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). Regarding the phrase "joined with the *namaskāra*," some say that at the end of the vocative and at the end of the goddess's name, the word *namaḥ* should be appended; thus, *hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *śirase namaḥ*, and so on, the word *namaḥ* is to be used everywhere.

Others say it is the word "pada" (foot), because in that case there is no application of the word "namaḥ" together with the portion of the mantra. Having stated regarding Bālā: "O Goddess, one should perform the six-limbed [rite] by repeating [the mantra] twice in sequence," this section further specifies regarding Kumārī Tripureśānī: "and for the year-old [Kumārī], as before," according to the *Jñānārṇava*.

Since there is an absence of authoritative evidence for such conceptualization and because it is burdened by unnecessary complexity, it appears that the application beginning with "aiṃ namaḥ hṛdayāya namaḥ," "klīṃ namaḥ śirase svāhā," and so forth, is more appropriate. Regarding the mudrās in this context, the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* states: "One should place [the mantra] upon the heart using the three fingers excluding the little finger and the thumb."
The knower of mantras should place [the mudrā] on the head with the middle and ring fingers;
having placed the topknot with the thumb, he should place the armor with the ten fingers.
O Supreme Goddess, one should perform the placement of the eyes with the heart-mantras;
then, O Dear One, one should place the weapon-mantra with the index and middle fingers.
With the eight [syllables] beginning with *śiraḥ*, he states the mantras for Vaśinī and the others.
In the Jñānārṇava.
O Dear One, one should write the seed-syllable at the end of the vowels, joined with the fire [Ra], the letter ending in Pha [Ba], and the earth [La];
it is adorned with the beauty of the left ear [U] and marked with the Bindu and Nāda.
O Goddess of virtuous vows, one should worship Vaśinī, the deity of speech.
The syllable *ra* is fire (*vahni*), the syllable *va* is the end of *pha* (*phānta*), the letter *la* is the earth (*kṣamā*), and the vowel *ū* is the left ear (*vāmakarṇa*).
Thus, in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"One should worship the supreme Kāmeśvarī at the end of the *ka*-group, joined with the digit (*kalā*)."

In the *Jñānārṇava*: "At the end of the *ca*-group [consonants], one should worship Mohinī, the deity of speech, who is conjoined with the fourth vowel [au] and the syllable following the letter *dh* [namely, *ṇa*]."
The letter *na* is the end of *dhā*, and the letter *va* is water (*nīra*).
O Goddess of the Gods, at the end of the *ṭa*-group, it is joined with the letter *ya* situated in the mouth;
enriched by the moon of the left ear and the *bindu*, this is Vimalā, the Sovereign of Speech.
The letter *ya* is wind, and the letter *la* is the mouth of water.
In the *Saṃhitā*:
"At the end of the *ta*-group [is] the one whose nature consists of the time of *ja*, fire, the left eye, and a digit of the moon."
O Goddess, one should worship the letters of the *advan* [group]; it is said that they are at the end of the *pavarga*.
It is like the sky, dark blue as the earth, and adorned with the moon of the wind.
"By this, the victorious worship is performed. *Jaḥ* is its essential form (*svarūpa*), followed by the group of consonants (*vargya*). *Kāla* is the letter *ma*.
"The third *kūrca*, joined with the fourth vowel of fire (*ra*) in the belly, and conjoined with *nāda* and *bindu*"—according to the statement in the *Śrīkrama*.

The sky is the letter *ha*, the individual soul (*jīva*) is the letter *sa*, the earth is the letter *la*, water is the letter *va*, and air is the letter *ya*; these are joined with the letter *jha*. This is according to the statement in the *Vāmakeśvara*: "It is pierced above. Furthermore, in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"At the end of the *ya*-group, [the letter] joined with fire (*ra*), the end of the vowels (*au*), and air (*ya*)."
One should fully worship Māyādyā, the goddess of speech, who is the sovereign of all.
The letter *jha* is at the end [of the consonant group].

According to the statement in the *Vāmakeśvara*, "one should extract the fourth from the *modinī* group," the vowel *ū* is also to be applied here. This is because of the statement in the *Śrīkrama*, "joined with the sixth vowel," which refers to the *māyā* (the nasal bindu).
One should worship Kaulinī, who is situated within the fire of the letter *kṣa*, encircled by the fourth seed-syllable (*v*), and pervaded by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*.
O Great Goddess, one should place it at the end of the *śa*-group for the accomplishment of all aims.
"The letters *a* and *ma* are the essential nature; O Goddess, Kaulinī is the fifth, situated as the seed-syllable of Time (*kālavīja*).

This is according to the statement of the *Vāmakeśvara*. Here, because the term "Vāgdevatā" (Goddess of Speech) is employed everywhere, Vaśinī and the others should be understood as being joined with those terms. And in that regard, [the letter *va*] is Vaśinī, according to the statement of Āpastamba: "As heard in the case of *vihāra*... and so forth.

"Salutation to Vāgdevatā"—thus it is seen in many places. According to the statement in the *Śrīkrama*, "One should place the *vyūhaka* [on the feet], the two ankles (*gulpha*), the *śa*-group, and Kaulinī situated on the thighs; one should place the Supreme (*parā*) [starting from the form]," the meaning is that one should perform the placement starting from the form (the feet) up to the two ankles. And here, there is the nature of the letters of the Mātṛkā and the eight groups (*vargāṣṭaka*).

"Endowed [with the powers], one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Vaśinī Mātṛkā, endowed with the eight seed-syllables"— according to this statement from the *Jñānārṇava*, since Vaśinī and the others are themselves the form of the Mātṛkā, it is stated in the *Vāmakeśvara* and other texts that the placement of the Mātṛkā is accomplished by the placement of those [powers] alone. And thus, in the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*:
"Having become pure in every respect, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of Vaśinī.
Having thus introduced the subject with "In all tantras," and having fully described Vaśinī and the others, [the text continues] with "The three *kūṭas* of Vālā," and so forth.

From the mention of the purification of the hands (*kara-śuddhi*), the four seats (*catuṣṭaya-āsana*), the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅga-nyāsa*), and the measures (*mātrā*), it is understood that these alone are necessarily to be performed. For this very reason, even in the *Vāmakeśvara-tantra*, there is only the mention of these measures. When establishing the sequence (*krama*), that which has been stated [there] should be adopted. Furthermore, although the word "atha" (now/then) is employed as an indicator of immediate succession (*ānantarya*),...
The placement [of mantras] on the hands alone is appropriate for the purification of the hands;
for it is stated in the *Nāradapañcarātra*: "Having first performed the placement on the hands, one should then perform the placement on the body.
For this very reason, elsewhere the purification of the hands and so forth is prescribed by the Teacher using the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) alone. [This applies] to the *vidyā* itself.

Because it is the cause of supreme purification, the term *bhūtaśuddhi* (purification of the elements) is used here; or alternatively, because that [purification] was taught by the venerable teachers in the section on Yoga with reference to a specific type of practitioner.
Regarding the phrase "one should perform the deposition (*nyāsa*) with eight [syllables]," immediately thereafter, in the *Vāmakeśvara Tantra*, [it says] "in a vessel of gold," and so forth.

One should place the supreme *argha* offering upon the *sādhāra*. It is mixed with *rocanā*, *candana*, *kāśmīra*, and "light" (*laghu*) musk; for *karpūra-reṇumāra* is indeed *karpūra-candrabhasma*, according to the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa*: "In the sense of 'quick,' *laghu* is neuter; in the sense of 'heavy' (*guru*), it is masculine. Its synonym is as follows:
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Having fashioned a square mandala on the left side,
one should place the yantra upon it and then pour the conch-water there."
Having honored [the deity] with pure water, one should perform worship accompanied by the causal [mantra].
Having worshipped the six limbs there, O Dear One, this is for the sake of the common purpose.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the characteristics of the special arghya (offering water):
between the self and the Śrīcakra, there should be a square mandala.
With water from the general arghya vessel, the preceptor, kneeling on the ground,
should worship there upon the mandala a triangle, a circle, and a hexagon.
Then, having visualized the Fire there, one should worship that which consists of the Yantra;
O Supreme Goddess, as before, one should worship the triangle situated in the center.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship there in the triangle with the individual syllables of the *kūṭa*;
one should worship the six limbs by repeating [the mantra] twice within the hexagons.
O beloved, one should also place a vessel made of gold or silver;
upon it, one should draw the Sūryabudhnya yantra in the form of the Sun, as previously described.
One should worship, as before, in sequence with the syllables both collectively and individually;
especially filling it completely, O Dear One, with the liquid of the moon.
Having drawn the yantra as before, O Dear One, he who visualizes a triangle there with Trikūṭā situated in its center considers it as worshipped by the three peaks.

In the [six] non-conversational [sections] and so forth, one should worship the six limbs by repeating twice the first letter of each class [of consonants], with *ha* and *kṣa* as the final [letters], within the six triangles.
Having propitiated the self with the *haṃsa*, one should worship with bliss;
thereupon, one should mutter the root-vidyā consisting of sixteen syllables, which is supreme.

Then, having offered incense, lamps, and food offerings, and having performed prostrations and the *arghya* offering, one should display the mudrās there; thus, one becomes manifest as the embodiment of Brahman.
8b) One should sprinkle oneself with that [water], as well as the various articles for worship;
one should perform sprinkling everywhere so that everything becomes composed of Brahman.

Within one's own *śrīcakra*, on the southern side of the *cakra*—just as in the *Ṣaṭśatika* it is said, "on the southern side of the *cakra* is the mandala of this mudrā"—one should meditate upon the fire consisting of the three *kalās* and worship it as before, in the manner of the installation of the water-pot (*kumbha*); such is the connection. In that regard, the worship of the *kalās* of the fire has been described as follows:
In the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*, the ten digits (*kalā*) of Fire are to be known as Bhūmi, Ātman, Tritat, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā,
and likewise Havyavahā and Kavyavahā;
they bestow the fruits of the ten dharmas.

"One should worship those joined with the vowels in sequence, from the lowest to the highest"— this explains what was stated as "one should worship there," meaning that one should worship the *trikūṭā* by repeating it twice in both places. Regarding the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the worship of the limbs in the directions— namely, the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, and the center— is according to the sequence taught by Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
"Golden [is the vessel]... one should never have a vessel made that is less than eight finger-breadths," according to the statement in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*. Likewise, in the *Mahāvarāha Tantra*:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the auspicious rite for the coconut."
In ancient times, indeed, a vessel was fashioned by the wise Viśvāmitra.
The vessel of Viśvāmitra, however, is the most excellent among all vessels;
in it, one should worship the gods, the Siddhas, and the goddesses in every way.
Merely by the sight of him, O beloved, he will undoubtedly uplift twenty-one generations of his family, even though he remains a householder.
Upon seeing a coconut vessel, even the sins of killing a Brahmin as well as those of betraying trust are destroyed; all sin perishes.
O Maheśānī, he who gives away ten million maidens as well as hundreds of gold pieces when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, [attains great merit].
The fruit of that [merit] is multiplied ten millionfold by the gift of the value of a coconut;
in the absence of such a recipient, one should worship it in other vessels.
O Goddess of the gods, having offered the arghya vessel, the hosts of deities beginning with Brahmā,
all the yoginīs, being delighted, dance and bestow accomplishment (siddhi).
Likewise, in the Devīpurāṇa: "Vessels made of gold, silver, copper, wood, clay, or stone, as well as vessels of gems and other materials, should be marked with auspicious lines."
One should arrange for the offering of water (argha), food (naivedya), worship, and so forth, as well as the presentation of the sacrificial oblation (bali).
Regarding the specific type of wood, the *Kālikā Purāṇa* states: "Or [the vessel] may be made of sacrificial wood. Likewise:
"If all [other materials] are unavailable, however, it may be made of clay, provided it is fashioned by one's own hand."
One should provide a seat, a vessel for the arghya offering, and water for washing the feet.

"Since copper is superior even to gold in every respect as a vessel," thus it is said. By the passage beginning with "having the form of the sun," the worship of its *kalā* (energy) is described; that was stated in the *Ṣaṭśalya*:
"Having established the *argha* vessel upon the seat of the vessel there..."
Having drawn the maṇḍala, one should worship the digit (kalā) therein.
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīcī, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumṇā,
Bhogadā, Viśvā, Rodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā.
The twelve [signs] of the Sun are to be known as bestowing the fruits of all desires.
The six [vowels] beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*, which bestow the earth and are served by the command (*ājñā*), are as follows:
"Salutation to *Kabham* for Tāpinī," and so forth, as previously described; thus Dakṣiṇāmūrti has also said.
The supreme vessel, worshipped with perfumes and the like, is fumigated with incense.
Having established it upon the mechanical device, one should draw the previously mentioned yantra.
In that very same way, O beautiful one, one should worship after uttering the Kāmakūṭa mantra;
there, one should especially worship with a vessel made of copper.
"Specifically," as stated in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*:
"Mixing sugar with milk, ghee, and honey,
fill the *argha* vessel and worship the mandala of Soma."
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati,
Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Aṅgadā.
The digits born of the self (Svarajā) are Pūrṇā, Apūrṇā, Amṛtā, and Kāmadāyinī.
[One should recite] "aṃ, obeisance to Amṛtā," and so forth. In the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*:
"And the Five Jewels (*pañcaratna*) are in the center of that; thereafter are *glūṃ* and *slūṃ*."
One should draw a triangle in the center with the five goddesses: *mlūṃ*, *plūṃ*, and *nlūṃ*.

In the midst of that, within the *kalā*, in the four directions and in the center, one should worship with "Glūṃ, obeisance to Gaganaratna," and so forth. The meaning is that one should meditate upon the triangle consisting of three lines starting from *A* and *Ka* (the *akathādi*), and worship as before. From the west to the southeast are the sixteen vowels beginning with *A*; from the southeast to the northeast are the sixteen consonants beginning with *Ka*.

Having visualized the sixteen [elements] beginning with space (kha) from the northeast to the west, one should contemplate *hasau* in the center; thus, by means of the eight-syllable *haṃsa*, it is stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"First uttering the *praṇava*, likewise the supreme word *haṃsaḥ*."
Therefore, O Goddess, I am that Śiva; I am declared to be this group of Vasus.

According to the *Prapañcasāra*, "Haṃsapada" with the *visarga* is the *tāra* (Oṃ), and "Śakti" is the *ajāpī* (Hrīṃ). [The text says] "with bliss," meaning with the mantra of Ānandabhairava. He himself states the mantra: "Having worshipped with these mantras, one should sacrifice to Ānandabhairava."
Śiva (H), Candra (S), the end of Mātṛkā (M), Kāla (K), Śakra (L), Ambu (V), and Vahni (R);
and Vāyu (Y) joined with the left ear (Ū) and adorned with the Bindu (M).
Having uttered this seed-syllable (bīja) as well as Ānandabhairava ending in -ṅ,
joined with the crest-mantra (śikhā-mantra), one should again write down the seed-syllable.
One should form the Moon (Candra), one should form this (I), and one should join Karṇi with the left eye (Vāmākṣi).
Then [one offers] Sudhā to the Goddess with *vauṣaṭ*; one is oneself Ānandabhairava.
Having worshipped the Moon with this, the water-pot shall become worthy of worship.

The letter *ha* is the head; *sa* is the moon; *kṣa*, the end of the Mātṛkā, is Kāla; *ma* is Śakra; *la* is water; *va* is fire; *ra* is wind; in the left ear is the long *ū*; *śikhā* (the crest) is *vaṣaṭ*. "Candra" refers to the union of Śiva and the Moon; in the left eye is the long *ai*; [this is] the root-vidyā.
One should recite [the mantra] seven times. Having offered [the oblation] and displayed the *mudrās*, such as the *saṃkṣobha* and others;
according to the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*, the remainder is that one should likewise place the vessel for the *arghya*, the *pādya*, and the *ācamana*.
In the *Śāradātilaka*:
"To the north of the *argha* water, the *pādya* and the *ācamanīyaka* should be prepared."
Thus ends the second wave in the *Saubhāgyataraṅgiṇī* composed by the venerable Mukunda.
Regarding another *argha* offering, it is stated in the *Vāmakeśvara*:
"Then, [one should perform] the meditation beginning with 'lotus-like' (*padmanibhām*). In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Thus, having deposited [the mantras] upon the body, one becomes the true self of all, the accomplisher of everything."
Meditating upon the stainless reality that deludes the three worlds.
The supreme consciousness, the mistress of all worldly transactions without exception,
possessing the brilliance of a thousand rising suns and the luster of a pomegranate flower.
The Supreme Goddess, who resembles the Javā flower, possesses a luster like a ruby;
she shines with the brilliance of sparkling gems and has the hue of molten gold.
Her two feet, adorned with sprout-like soles shaped like the petals of a red lotus, are graced by anklets fashioned from priceless jewels.
When she, the sovereign lady, whose thighs were as delicate as the graceful trunk of a plantain tree, was resplendent with the brilliance of the jewel set upon her finger-ring.
Adorned with red garments shimmering upon her rounded hips,
she pervades the entire circle of the three worlds with the radiance flashing from her jeweled silks.
He spoke to her who was resplendent in a divine bodice, variegated with jewels,
and who was resonant with the tinkling of small bells and rubies that adorned her face.
She possessed a waist that was imperceptible, a deep navel, and an exceedingly slender belly;
she was graced with the vine-like line of hair and endowed with the great fruit of her breasts.
Adorned with the circles of her well-rounded, high, and prominent breasts,
she shone brilliantly with the weight of necklaces shimmering with priceless pearls.
Adorned with excellent ornaments such as necklaces and girdles glowing with the luster of the nine gems,
her ears were made beautiful by the ornament of sacred learning, and her cheeks were like clusters of blossoming jasmine.
She possesses the luster of earrings resembling the rising sun;
she has a face like the full moon, a countenance like a lotus, and lips like coral.
She surpassed the splendor of the essence of Brahma-vidya by the sweetness of her smile; she was a beautiful-browed, lotus-eyed woman whose quivering eyebrows were like the staff of the God of Love.
Adorned with an excellent jewel-tilaka shining upon her forehead,
she wears tiny bells upon the surface of her crown fashioned from pearls and rubies.
She wears a crown from which the shimmering digit of the moon radiates; she possesses three eyes and four vine-like arms that gleam like coral creepers.
Her mouth was filled with betel-leaf mixed with whole camphor,
and she was adorned with a necklace fashioned from coral vines and endowed with the quality of fine silk.
The second [verse] describes her as having the luster of the crescent moon, capable of attracting the moon,
possessing a bow made of sugarcane whose string consists of the qualities that have become bees, and being endowed with true knowledge.
I bow to the Mother, who is composed of all the gods, who is beautiful with every auspicious fortune, and who bears the five arrows shining as pure as a lotus.
I bow to the eternal Vidyā, who embodies all sacred fords, who fulfills all desires, who consists of all scriptures, and who is honored by all the Āgamas.
The Goddess who consists of all sacred traditions, who is served by all abodes,
who is composed of all bliss, and who is the supreme consciousness subject to the power of knowledge.
Regarding the visualization of the weapons: the first two are in the upper left hands, and the other two are in the lower ones.
However, according to the *Daśapaṭalī*, the right hands are said to hold a goad and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), while the left hands grant desired boons (*varada*);
and in the *Uttaraṣaṭka*, it is stated that the left hand is joined with the gesture of fearlessness and the right hand is the boon-granting gesture.

Regarding Bhuvaneśī, since she is designated as such, one may contemplate her weapons exactly as desired; in this very way, her sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is also established. By the phrase "consisting of all the gods" (*sarvadevamayī*), it is understood that through hearing her and so forth, one obtains the merit produced by hearing all the gods and so forth. In this manner, the other [perfections] are also supreme according to their respective fitness. Thus:
In the Vāmakeśvara [Tantra]: "Having remembered the Great Mudrā of Tripura in the form of a vehicle, one should invoke her,
O Fortunate One, with the Vidyā joined by the salutation."
The supreme practitioner, having meditated upon Mahātripurasundarī in the center of the wheel according to what was previously described, should then perform the worship.
The Mahātripuramudrā is the Trikhaṇḍā mudrā; for it is said in the Jñānārṇava: "Indeed, by means of the Trikhaṇḍā mudrā. In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
"Form three separate staffs from the previously mentioned Yonimudrā."
[One should perform it] with the two thumbs, the two little fingers, and the two middle fingers, respectively.
This is the mudrā named Trikhaṇḍā, for the ritual of the knowledge of Tripura;
it was spoken by Bhairavī herself in her form as Āvāhanā.
She is mounted upon the seed-syllable, seated upon the foremost seat of Āghā, the accomplisher of all aims; such is the rite for the invocation of the goddesses.

The seed-syllable *hasa* consists of the letters *ha* and *sa*; then one should perform the first established self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*) vidyā. The third [syllable], however, is joined with the letter *ra* and *ha*. In the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*: "O Goddess, one should display the mudrās and worship in three ways with libations."
Having propitiated [the deity] with all mental and manifest auspicious services,
ending with incense, lamps, and food offerings, one should again display the mudrās.
Having satisfied [the deities] once more, O Goddess of the gods, one should worship the Tithinityā;
the mudrās beginning with Saṃkṣobhā should be performed, and the libation (tarpaṇa) with the Tatvamudrā.
Having again offered libations three times with the *tattvamudrā*, [one should proceed].
For it has been stated by [the author] himself: "This is declared to be the *tattvamudrā* formed by the thumb and the ring finger. Regarding the substance, the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā* says:
"And one should satisfy [the deities] with substances of honey and with ghee mixed with honey."
And another should satisfy the Supreme Deity with nectar-like substances.

"By means of services such as the *arghya* offering and so forth. Regarding the sequence for presenting these, Somaśambhu says: "Having first uttered [the mantra] preceded by the heart [mantra], one should present the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the other offerings."
One should offer "namaḥ," "svadhā," "svāhā," and "vauṣaṭ" respectively;
[the water for] the feet is offered to the pair of lotus-feet, and the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) to the mouth.
One should offer the *arghya*—consisting of flowers, *durvā* grass, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*)—upon the head of the Deity with the mantra:
"O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī," at the end of the root-vidyā.

One should offer water together with *śyāmāka* grain, *dūrvā* grass, and lotuses, saying: "This is for your feet; obeisance. One should know that the *arghya* and other offerings are likewise performed with the third section [of the mantra]. For the other services (*upacāra*), there is no [use of] the word "obeisance" (*namaḥ*). O Goddess, one should offer the flower with the mudrā known as Jñāna.
10b) "The Knowledge Mudrā (jñānamudrā) is proclaimed through the joining of the thumb and forefinger"— this is the specific detail stated in the *Jñānārṇava*. Likewise, in the *Jñānārṇava*:
At this time, O Goddess, one should worship the daily Tithinityā;
O Maheśvarī, these are the Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Vicitrā.
On the full moon day of the month of Prajāpatya (Śrāvaṇa), one should worship the deity in the form of the lunar day (tithi),
having visualized the great triangle in the sequence of front, right, and left.
One should draw five lines there in sequence;
one should contemplate those beginning with the letter 'A' and ending at the ears on the right side.
Then, having written the group of five beginning with Dīrghakarṇa on the eastern line,
one should thereafter write the group beginning with Śakti on the northern line.
One should worship the sixteen measures ending with the anusvāra, and the sixteenth in the visarga;
O Goddess of gods, the sixteen Nityās are proclaimed [to be worshipped] by moving counter-clockwise.
O Daughter of the Mountain, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) until the full moon (paurṇamāsī),
one should worship each Nityā daily and shall attain great good fortune.
O Maheśānī, during the dark fortnight, one should worship the circle of lunar days (tithi-maṇḍala),
beginning with Vicitrā, O Varārohā, until Kāmeśvarī is reached.
O Supreme Goddess, the sixteen digits (kalās) of the moon should be worshipped in reverse order during the waning phase, O Mistress of the Gods, according to their sequence.
O Great Goddess, by following the instruction of the Guru,
one attains good fortune after worshipping the Nityās, beginning with Kāmeśvarī, in their proper sequence.
O Goddess, for the sake of good fortune, one should worship the Tithinityās three times;
furthermore, for the sake of auspiciousness, one should worship the Śrī Tripurā Vidyā.

The great triangle has a triangle at its extremity. The [letters] ending with *karṇa* are those ending with *ukāra*. By that, the five beginning with Kāmeśvarī are in the southern corner from the first corner to the southeast (*āgneya*). The group of five beginning with Mahāvidyeśvarī, starting from the long *karṇa*, is on the eastern line from the southeast to the northeast (*īśāna*). [Then] the [group] beginning with Śakti...
The pentad beginning with the blue banner (*nīlapatākā*) is in the northern line, starting from the northeast corner (*īśāna*).

They say that the power (*śakti*) is "eḥ" by way of counter-clockwise rotation for the Goddess; however, this is untenable because it is impossible to visualize [it] due to the presence of the *bindu-cakra* (the circle of the bindu) within the eight corners and so forth.

Because of its extreme smallness, it is impossible for it to undergo great drying; and because it lies on the western diagonal line from south-east to north-west, it is impossible for it to follow the sequence from south-east to north-east. Therefore, having visualized a great triangle outside the four-eyed [square], one should [draw] lines from the corners to the south-east, then to the north-east, and then from that corner to the end of the north-west.
The ultimate meaning is that one should worship five times five. Regarding the statement "the sixteenth in the center," Dakṣiṇāmūrti says:

"In the center, one should worship the Goddess who consists of the Goddesses, the Great Nityā. This means that having extracted the fifteen Nityās—the Goddess who consists of the Goddesses, whose nature is the fifteen Nityās—this entity is the essence of all.

"It is designated as Tripura," because it is so stated by [the scripture] itself. Having thus worshipped all [the goddesses], he speaks again of the worship on each respective lunar day (tithi) for her who takes the form of that specific tithi: "When there is an increase in the number of days for the first lunar day (pratipat), on which of the two days should one perform the worship? It should be understood that one should perform the worship of the two Nityās on whichever day [the practice] is repeated."
11a) "They are to be worshipped in their respective places. Furthermore, this [practice] is indeed obligatory (*nitya*). In the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*, however, it is stated:
"One should worship the Nityās, beginning with Kāmeśvarī, upon the limbs of the Goddess. In the *Tantrarāja* as well, it is exactly the same. Likewise:
In the *Jñānārṇava*: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme *Nityāmaṇḍala*.
Kāmeśvarī is the Great *Nityā*, who brings all the worlds under her control."
And at the end of "vārāṃtara," O Kāmeśvarī, one should write the word *pada*;
at the end of "icchākāmaphala," one should write the word *prade sarva*.
Then one should utter *satvavaśam*, the state of the wise one who pervades the entire world;
at the end of the agitation, one should utter the word "kavi" and write two *hūṃ* syllables.
Having drawn the five arrows with the withdrawal [process] upon the maiden,
this eternal Kāmeśvarī has been described here incidentally, O beloved.

"In the two eternal *hūṃ* syllables, [there is] *samīvilaḥ*; at the end of the agitation (*kṣobha*), O Supreme Goddess, there are the poet (*kavi*) and the arrows *hūṃ hūṃ*. This is because it is in agreement with the statement of Dakṣiṇāmūrti. Likewise, one should write the Vāgbhava syllable at the end of the word *bhaga*, followed by *bhuge* and *bhagini*.
O you whose belly is the bhaga, O you who are at the end of the bhaga, O garland of the bhaga, O bringer of the bhaga;
O you who are in the secret place of the bhaga, O you who are at the edge of the bhaga, O you who are at the edge of the yoni—thereafter, the bhagas.
And at the very end, O Blessed Śaṅkarī, there is the word *nipātini*;
then, in the form of the *bhaga*, one should write the two eyes, blue and yellow.
