One should always write "nityaklinne bhagaprānte svarūpe" [O you who are eternally moist at the edge of the vulva, in your own form]; one should write "bhagāni me sthāpayeti varade" [Establish the vulvas for me, O giver of boons].
O Netre, O Sure, O Te, O Bhagā; you who are moistened, you who are the moisture, and you who are the fluid; then, O Mistress of the Yoni of all beings, moisten and cause to flow!
Amoghe bhagaviśve cakṣu bhakṣo bhaya sarva ca | Satvān bhageśvariṃ brūyād vāgbhavaṃ vlūṃ jamādikaṃ ||
BHE & VLŪ & MO & VLŪ & CA HE & VLŪ & CA HE & KLĪNNE CA,
and thereafter SARVĀṆI CA BHAGĀNYANTE ME VAŚAṂ CĀNAYA.
Having written the female seed-syllable (strīvīja) at the end of Hara, the syllable consisting of the power (bala), and Bhuvaneśī— this is the Vidyā Bhagamālinī.
"O Mistress of the Fortune of All Beings"—this is the address to the Goddess. *Ja* and so forth, with *vlūṃ*; thus, *jaṃ vlūṃ*.
Joined with *vale*, one should utter the supreme seed-syllable (*parābīja*): "O Ever-Moist One, O You Who Flow with Intoxication."
The mantra ending with "agnijāyā" (svāhā) is declared as "nityaklinne yamī."
Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should likewise draw a pair of hooks;
in their center, O Goddess, one should write the syllable consisting of Paromā.
One should write it joined with the fire-syllable (Ra), diminished by the group of three vowels,
endowed with the fourteen vowels, and marked individually with the bindu and nāda.
The mantra of Bheruṇḍā, when joined with the wife of Vahni (the syllable *svāhā*), bestows the fruit [of its practice].

In the middle of that [mantra], the syllable *bharaum* is conjoined between two *aṅkuśas* (hooks). This is because of the statement of Dakṣiṇāmūrti: "Having uttered the syllable *oṃ*, it is well-encircled by the two *aṅkuśas*."
Having uttered "Bhuvaneśī" followed by "Vahni-vāsinī" in the dative case,
ending with the heart-mantra (namaḥ), O Goddess, this is the mantra of Vahni-vāsinī, who is eternal.
The Praṇava, Bhuvaneśānī, and the syllable whose essence is the fruit—
this is the Visarga; thereafter is the Moon (Sa), [placed] in the ever-moist, intoxicating fluid.
This Vidyā, conjoined with the wife of Fire (Svāhā), bestows all sovereignty.

"Mahāvidyeśvarī is eternal. [The mantra is formed by] joining *pha-re-mi-ti* with the letter *sa*, which is like the moon. Having uttered the supreme seed-syllable (*parābīja*), one should address Śivadūtī joined [with it].
O Goddess, this heart-mantra is the messenger (*dūtī*) that grants all desires.
Having uttered the seed-syllable Oṃ, one should write the supreme armor (kavaca);
having written the mantra of one's own chosen deity, one should also write the female seed-syllable (strīvīja).
The syllable *hūṃ* is the weapon for hurling; this is the twelve-syllable vidyā.
This vidyā named Tvaritā is difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
The Kulasundarī is indeed composed of all lion-thrones;
one should likewise enclose the Nityabhairavī with the Vālā.
O Goddess of the gods, she who consists of the syllables of Indra is considered the eternal Pañcavāṇā;
O Beloved, this Aparā is eternal through the five-syllabled seed-mantras of the arrows.

The Goddess herself spoke of Nityabhairavī: "O Mistress of the Gods, having written the *bījas* of Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, and Kākinī from the [four] ages (*yuga*), one should join them with the Moon and the Sun."
O Goddess, one should write the third seed-syllable, joined with the first letter 'a' and 'na', adorned with another 'ī', and endowed with the vowel 'śakra' (u).
O Daughter of the Mountain, this triad is pervaded by Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā.
"Kalā is visarga; [the mantra] joined with bindu and nāda consists of two aghas (the syllable *aghora*) and the last [syllable] like the vasarga," according to the statement of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Of this very vidyā, the six syllables situated in their proper order—
O mature one, this knowledge, when free from error, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

"The goddess Bhairavī is the first [of] Nityā and the others. The seed-syllables (*bīja*) are simply the initial letters of Ḍākinī and the others. The connection is as follows: having written the two seed-syllables *sa* and *ha* for the moon and sun immediately after the pair beginning with Lākinī, one should join them. Regarding "the reversed ones beginning with *ha* and ending with *ḍa*," Dakṣiṇāmūrti says that one should write the five arrows ending with the letter *ta*, and then [divide them] into two.
Endowed with fire (Ra),
adorned with the bindu and the dot by means of the left eye of Ananta (Ū),
it is the Kāma-bīja (Klīm); then, beginning with Kāla (Ka) and so forth, it is joined with earth (La).
One should write in sequence [the mantra] ending with the letter *ma*, enriched by the long ear (*dīrghakarṇa*), the moon (*indu*), and the drop (*bindu*);
then the letter *da* at the end of the letter *u*, followed by *kāla* and so forth, beginning with the letter *va*.
"Up to the end of *ajapā* is *saḥ*.
Then [one recites] the *praṇava*, the *bhuvaneśī*, and the syllable consisting of the fruit;
then the second [syllable] consisting of *mrūm*, and then the *bhuvaneśī-aṅkuśa*."
Having extracted the word *nitya* and the vocative *madadrave*,
one should likewise take the armor (*kavaca*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*), as well as the *vidyā* [mantra] of Nīlapatākinī.
The syllable *repha* (the letter *r*) is conjoined [with the previous], and it is the second with respect to the preceding seed-syllable. Likewise, in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"Adorned with the head, the moon, the void, the fire, Rudra, and the vowel."
One should write "Vijaye namo," which is pervaded by the bindu, nāda, and kalā.
The letter *kha* is its own form, and the letter *pha* is the protector (*pānta*). In the Jñānārṇava:
"One should write the seed-syllable of Tārā conjoined with the Moon and Varuṇa."
Then, O Goddess, on the fourth [day], one should draw Sarvamaṅgalā.
O Goddess, this mantra ending with the heart [syllable] is eternally auspicious in every way.
The seed-syllable *tāra* is the syllable *oṃ* with the bindu (*auṃ*).
12a) *Tāraṃ hṛdbhagavatyante jvālāmālini devi ca*.
And having uttered it twice, at the very end [one says]: "O you who effect the dissolution of all beings!"
Having written "jātavedasi," one should utter the word "jvalanti";
then one should write the pair "jvāla" and "prajvāla," followed by two "hūṃ" syllables.
The mantra consists of the three fire-seeds, *hūṃ*, and the weapon-syllable accompanied by *svāhā*.
O Great Goddess, this is the supreme Nityā Jvālāmālinikā.
"Jvālā" is also said to be a pair (*yuga*), meaning a pair of flames (*jvālayugma*), as stated in the *Saṃhitā*.
"Hūṃ" is the short fire-syllable, and it is also stated in that same source that the armor (*kavaca*) is threefold.
[It is] the end of the *ka*-group, the end of the vowels, adorned with the vowel of Indra (the letter *e*).
O Supreme Goddess, she is wondrous, pervaded by the bindu, nāda, and kalā.
"Dakṣiṇāmūrti says that one should write the mantra ending with the *ka*-group [consonants] and ending with the vowel *ca*, adorned with the *cakrānugraha* (the *bindu* of the wheel) and the *bindu*.
He stated this in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* as a synonym."
Then, one should join the seed-syllable of Śrī, namely Hṛllekhā, with the Nāda at the beginning.
At the end of each name, the word "Śrī" should be added, followed by the statement "I worship the sandals" (pādukāṃ pūjayāmi).
By this sequential method, all the Mothers are to be worshipped.
The word "ca" (and) includes the words beginning with "namaḥ" for worship and other rites; thus, there should be a salutation such as "I worship the sandals.
In the case of *homa* and libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should recollect [the mantra] ending with "svāhā," saying "I satisfy [the deity]."
Because it is stated thus by himself at the beginning:

"I worship" (*pūjayāmi*) and "I satisfy" (*tarpayāmi*) should be understood [to apply] in their respective places due to their suitability. Therefore, it should be known that first there are two seed-syllables (*bīja*), then each one of the vowels, then the mantra, and then the name. When "O Mothers of All" (*sarvamātaraḥ*) is uttered...
Even in the *Ratna*, this is the very same method; for this reason alone, the notion that "the worship of the *kalās* is the destruction of sin" is refuted. Likewise, in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"At this time, O Goddess, the wise one should fully worship the Guru."
They say the center is triangular; at the two junctions, one should worship the lineage of gurus in three ways.
First, O Goddess, one should worship those called *parā*, who are divided into *parā* and *aparā*; then, O Beloved, one should worship the *aparā* in three ways and worship the Guru.

Know, O fair-faced one, that the divine current (divyaugha) consists of seven supreme [beings]; those known as the "higher-lower" are the current of the perfected ones (siddhaugha). Now listen, O beloved, to the human current (mānavaugha).
"In the afternoon" and "at midday" refer to the bindu and the western triangle respectively.
As it is stated in the Saṃhitā:
"One should worship the Guru-maṇḍala in the center of Vimalā and Jayinī."
The persons are proclaimed to end with the word Ānandanātha.
O Supreme Goddess, those ending in vowels and long vowels (am, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai, o, au) should be known as feminine;
the Gurus are to be worshipped with the three impurities for the sake of attaining perfection.
The *ali* (line) is a row, as stated in the *Yoginīrahasya*: "Then, O Goddess,
the wise one should worship the divine Guru, the Siddha, and the Mānada in sequence within the square,
starting from the east in rows."

One should worship the divine, the perfected, and the human [beings] starting from the east in rows. Then, O Goddess, as previously stated, one should worship in three rows starting from one's own position in the south, extending to the north and ending in the west. Thus is the square; the Goddess is situated in the west. Vimalā and Jayinī are in the triangle.
The middle of the two. And this is to be learned from one's own guru or from a similar source according to the tradition.
As it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
There are many lineages of transmission, and they must be understood through the succession of gurus;
O fair-faced one, I shall explain them for those disciples who do not know [them].
Having uttered "Salutation to the Gurus," one should write "Salutation to the Pādukās";
likewise, at the end of "Guru" and at the end of "Parama," one should also write "Salutation to the Gurus."
In the same way, one should pay homage to the sandals (pādukā) of these [deities], and likewise to the sandals of the Ācāryas;
similarly, the sandals of the Pūrvasiddhas are also twofold.
This is the lineage of gurus for all ordinary disciples and masters;
having worshipped this lineage of gurus, one becomes Śrī Tripurā herself.
One who is devoid of the lineage of gurus is indeed excluded from the ranks of men;
however, by means of a common lineage of gurus, one does not become excluded from the ranks.
The common gurus, however, are indeed equal across all divisions.
The phrase "ending with the guru" (gurvanta) is connected with the expression "salutation to the sandals" (pādukābhyo namaḥ).
"For these" means "Salutation to the sandals of the supreme guru"; likewise for the others as well.
For the previously perfected ones, it is twofold: "to the previously perfected ones" and "to the sandals of the previously perfected ones."

According to the *Prapañcasāra*, the seed-syllable beginning with Vāgbhava should be joined at the outset to all these varieties, such as Kāmarāja, Lopāmudrā, and others. Furthermore, the common gurus are to be worshipped in three rows, and finally, the four [special gurus] are worshipped.
After that, at the end of the lineage of human gurus (*mānavaugha*), one should worship the pair of one's own gurus.
After the Supreme [Guru], there is the Śrī Guru, and thereafter the Guru known as Parama.
O Maheśānī, one should worship one's own guru and the triad of gurus;
or else, at the end of the lineage of the Vāmānavas, one should worship one's own guru alone.
Then, O Maheśānī, the knower of the Śrīvidyā mantra should perform the eightfold covering;
in the center of the Śrīcakra, there is the worship of the limbs of the Goddess.
The worship of the limbs (*aṅga*) takes place in the intermediate directions—namely, the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest—and in the center.

This is because of the method to be described for the center of the triangle. In the center, [one worships] the Goddess; in the southeast, as desired, one should worship the Heart; and in the northeast, one should worship the Head.
The *śikhā* (crest) should be worshipped in the southwest, and one should worship the *kavaca* (armor) in the northwest;
having honored the *netra* (eye) in front, one should then worship the *astra* (weapon) in the cardinal directions.
In the Śāradātilaka:
The principal female forms possess rays that are white as frost, crystal, dark, blue, black, and reddish; they hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

Others say it is square. Regarding the measure of the limbs of the mantras known as the "Worship" (pūjā), which end with the word *namaḥ* and begin with the head (*śiras*) and so forth, it should be sought in the *Pūjākalpalatā*.
In the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, concerning the wheel that deludes the three worlds and consists of the form of the fifty letters:
O beautiful one, the ten Siddhis are manifest there and should be fully worshipped.
O beloved, they possess the luster of freshly smelted gold, hold nooses and goads,
and indeed bring forth great treasures, jewels, fine gold, and hidden hoards.
One should worship her who, with a lotus in her hand, bestows [attainments] upon practitioners;
she whose nature is the perfections of *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, and *mahimā*.
The mastery-siddhi is the manifestation of power; enjoyment shall likewise be according to one's desire.
One should worship so that the attainment-siddhi and all desired siddhis may become manifest.
On the right side of the door and likewise in the corner, according to that sequence,
both below and above, it is described in the Jñānārṇava.
O Supreme Goddess, O beautiful lady of the gods, the attainment of powers and the fulfillment of all desires are to be understood through the sequence of the downward and upward movements.

In the sequence stated in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*—namely, "the worship of the lords of the directions: below in the southwest (Nairṛti), above in the northeast (Īśāna); the lord of serpents below and above in the center; Viṣṇu in the southwest (Nairṛti), Brahmā in the northeast (Īśvara)"—it is taught that [Brahmā] is in the northwest (Vāyu). Alternatively, the term "lord of the southwest" (*naiṛteśvara*) may refer to the lotus-seated [Brahmā]. This is stated in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*.
In the southwest, situated at the western end, is Matta, white in form.

Between the northeast and the east are the Brahman-sages of firm vows—namely Brahmā and the ṛṣis. From this point upward, they should be worshipped in sequence by the teachers, beginning from the western direction.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, and likewise Indrāṇī are in the third [house].
Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, and the sixth, Vārāhikā,
as well as Cāmuṇḍā and Mahālakṣmī, [should be placed] in the other direction.
One should visualize all of them holding a noose and a goad,
and then [visualize them] in sequence holding a knowledge-staff (vidyā), a trident, a thunderbolt, a spear, a discus, and a mace.
O Supreme Goddess, for the sake of attaining perfection, one should sequentially visualize a garland of lapis lazuli and a lotus,
all endowed with every ornament.
By the western word, O Goddess, the center of the Self of the Goddess is indeed expressed;
when one extracts the wheel at the mouth of the northern [words], O Goddess.
"Then, O Goddess, the northern direction is indeed the eastern one; of this there is no doubt.
Thus it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*.
Since the northern directions and so forth are designated by the term "eastern" and so forth, one should worship them starting from that [east] by moving counter-clockwise around oneself. Likewise:
There, on the first line, one should worship Maṇimā and the others;
then, on the second line, one should worship Brahmāṇī and the others;
and there, on the third line, one should worship Saṃkṣobha and the others.

He states the [powers] beginning with *saṃkṣobha* in the *Jñānārṇava*: "One should worship *saṃkṣobha*, *drāvaṇa*, *ākarṣa*, *vaśya*, *unmāda*, *mahāṅkuśa*, *khecarī*, the one called *vījayoni*, and *trikhaṇḍā*."
Having worshipped on the left side as before in the directions beginning with Vāyavya,
[one worships] the five arrows, the five mudrās, and the syllable consisting of the two hands.
First is the seed-syllable of Rudrabhairavī, then Sadāśiva, and then the Vāgbhava alone; O Goddess, these four [syllables] are to be used in sequence.
Having worshipped the four mudrās, the eight seed-syllables, and the nine mudrās in sequence on the left side with sugarcane,
one should join them with the word "karomi" (I do).
The mantra also consists of the seed-syllable of Rudra-Bhairavī, the seed-syllable of Vijayā, and the seed-syllable of Sadāśiva;
this was stated by Manu and is mentioned in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā.
One should perform meditation while joined with this very [mantra].
The mantra-practitioner should display the mudrā which has the luster of a bandhūka flower;
beautiful with various ornaments, it brings the three worlds under control.
One should meditate upon all the hands bearing their respective mudrās, with Śrīvidyā at the forefront.

This [meditation] is established as being restricted to the Vidyās other than the Pañcamī (the five-syllabled mantra), because it is mentioned in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtikramasaṃhitā* and other texts within that specific context, such as the *Jñānārṇava*. In the *Jñānārṇava*:
Having worshipped these, one should worship the supreme Tripurā, the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśī),
who is situated before the power of atomization (aṇimā-siddhi) and who accomplishes all desires.
13b) O lotus-faced one, one should display the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā.
Regarding this, the Yoginī says in the *Hṛdaya*: "The mantra of this [mudrā] is..."
The first is the purification of the hands and so forth; the second is the protection of oneself;
O Goddess, the third follows immediately after that, which is seated upon the seat of the self.
Next, she is seated on the wheel-throne (cakrāsana), then established upon the throne of all mantras;
the sixth is in the middle on the perfected posture (siddhāsana)—she is Māyā, Lakṣmī, and likewise the Supreme One.
And that goddess is proclaimed as the seventh, Mūrtividyā;
the eighth is Vāhanīvidyā, and the ninth is the supreme Bhairavī.
The Root-Vidyā is proclaimed as that which brings the three worlds under its control;
it is Parāśakti, Bālā, and this very same Vidyā is the third form.
The connection is that the eighth is Bhairavī.
I shall state their names according to their actual meanings and in their proper order:
there, the first is the goddess Tripurā, and the second is Tripureśvarī.
And the third is likewise proclaimed as the goddess Tripurasundarī;
and the fourth is likewise proclaimed as the goddess Tripuravāsinī.
The fifth is Tripurāśrī, the sixth is Tripuramālinī,
the seventh is Tripurāsiddhā, and the eighth is Tripurātmikā.
But the ninth, O Maheśānī, is Mahātripurasundarī;
one should worship these in the nine wheels previously described, beginning with the Cakra.
Dakṣiṇāmūrti described meditation:
Tripurā has the luster of crystal, is adorned with pearls and red [gems],
and holds a book, a rosary, and an excellent lotus.

She, who is to be meditated upon for the sake of accomplishment, is the cutter away of great sins. She holds a book and other objects in her left hand, starting from the bottom and ending at the top, or as desired according to the logic of the situation.
He himself stated the definition of the mudrā: "One should join the two ring fingers and the two little fingers with the two middle fingers."
Then:
with the two thumbs joined like a moon and the two index fingers like a staff, this is the Saṃkṣobhiṇī Mahāmudrā; thereafter, one should offer worship according to the prescribed method.
He [the same author] states the second enclosure:
"That entire [goddess] unfolds within the *svara*-kalās in the *pūraka* wheel;
one should worship her in sequence, hidden from west to east in reverse order."
The eternal one who draws forth desire and the rest, likewise the attractor of the intellect,
the attractor of the ego, and likewise the attractor of sound.
Likewise, there is Sparśākarṣaṇikā; after that, Rūpākarṣaṇikā;
then the goddess Rasākarṣaṇikā, and similarly Gandhākarṣaṇikā.
Likewise, O beloved, there is the goddess Cittākarṣaṇikā, Dhairyākarṣaṇikā,
Smṛtyākarṣaṇikā, and Nāmākarṣaṇikā.
O Dear One, likewise there is the Atmākarṣaṇikā,
the eternal Amṛtākarṣaṇī, and thereafter the Śarīrākarṣaṇī.
O Goddess, one should constantly remember these eternal digits situated within the lunar orb; joined with the vowels, they perpetually shower down nectar.
Those who bestow the gift of a Kashmiri vessel filled with nectar, along with nooses, goads, and [the weapons] of the former deities;

a "Kashmiri vessel" refers to a cracked vessel. One should contemplate the weapons of the previous deities in reverse order, moving counter-clockwise from one's own left, according to the *Jñānārṇava*.
One should worship the goddess Cakreśī, the Mistress of Tripura, who bestows prosperity;
O Dear One, one should worship her in front of Kāmākarṣaṇarūpā.
Having displayed the Sarvavidrāvaṇī [mudrā], one should offer it;
Dakṣiṇāmūrti states the mantra-verse for the visualization (dhyāna).
O Great Goddess, she is beautiful with auspicious body-unguents and radiant with all the camphor;
she holds a noose and a goad in her right and left hands respectively.
He describes the mudrā: "Abounding in the splendor of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and possessing the perfect radiance of Sarasvatī;
[it is formed] by joining the middle and index fingers of this very same mudrā."
"Named Sarvavidrāvaṇī"—this refers to this [deity] Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī. "In the middle sanctuary"—thus he speaks of the third:
"In the wheel Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa, [one should worship] the groups of letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *lakṣa*."
The goddesses, who have the luster of bandhūka flowers, are to be worshipped most secretly.
One should visualize [the goddesses] holding noose and goad, with trembling blue lotuses in their hands,
in the four directions starting from the east and in the corners starting from the southeast, in due order.
Anaṅgakusumā, as well as Anaṅgamekhalā,
and likewise Anaṅgamadanā and Anaṅgamadanāturā.
And likewise Anaṅgarekhā, Vaśinī preceded by Anaṅga,
Anaṅgādyā, Aṅkuśā, Anaṅgamālinī, and Parameśvarī.
In the Jñānārṇava.
Then, O Goddess, one should worship Cakreśvarī Tripurasundarī at the tip of Anaṅgakusumā, she who bestows universal sovereignty.
O Goddess praised by the gods, one should display the mudrā of universal attraction;
having offered the worship of the wheel, one should then worship the fourth wheel.
O Sulocanā, one should form a wheel with the middle and index fingers joined;
this very mudrā is that which effects their attraction.
Dakṣiṇāmūrti describes the meditation on this Sarvavidrāviṇī: She is beautiful with the luster of a flower,
endowed with all ornaments, holding a book and a rosary of eight beads,
granting boons and fearlessness, accompanied by her attendants, and possessing a smiling countenance.
Dakṣiṇāmūrti speaks of the fourth:
"In the wheel that bestows great good fortune, which shines with the four castes,
reside the Yoginīs known as Saṃpradāpī, adorned with all ornaments."
All these mantra-deities are like indragopa insects and are full of pride;
they hold a noose, a goad, a mirror, and a vessel for nectar.
O Goddess, for the sake of spiritual accomplishment within the tradition, one should worship the Śaktis, who are all-auspicious and bear [the offerings], starting from the west in reverse order.
O Dear One, she is the power that agitates all, as well as the power that subdues all;
she is the power that accomplishes all aims and the one who brings delight to all.
The power that completely deludes, the one that causes the paralysis of all;
the power that paralyzes everything, the one that brings everything under control from every side.
The power that delights all, as well as the power that intoxicates all;
the power that accomplishes all aims, and the power that fulfills all prosperity.
The power consisting of all mantras, which brings about the destruction of all dualities; [as stated] in the Jñānārṇava:
"Then one should worship in front the power Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī."
To Cakreśvarī, the supreme bestower of siddhis, who dwells in Tripura.
Having displayed the Vaśyamudrā and offered [the oblation] immediately thereafter,
one should meditate upon the Goddess Tripuravāsinī as being similar to her; thus it is stated in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā.
By this Tripurasundarī, the Sovereign of the Wheel who agitates [all things].
Having formed the hands into the *puṭaka* shape, the two index fingers are made into hooks; then, by means of a revolving sequence, the two middle fingers go beneath them.
Following this sequence, the knower of mantras should join the two— the little finger and the ring finger—
and place them both at the base of the thumb, causing all [the other fingers] to rest.
"The mudrā that brings everything under control. He himself states the fifth [mudrā]:
"In the wheel that accomplishes all aims, adorned with the letter of the sky (Ha), [the deities] resemble the hibiscus flower and are embellished by shimmering blue [light]."
Possessing great good fortune and profound depth, with full, round, and firm breasts,
they have placed upon red baskets the ornaments desired by the practitioner.
One should meditate upon the Kulayoginīs as divine, composed of various jewels, with joyful faces, and bearing nooses and goads.
One should worship them in reverse order, beginning from the west; they bestow all accomplishments.
The Goddess is the giver of all accomplishments as well as the giver of all prosperity.
The Goddess who makes everything dear, the Goddess who brings about all auspiciousness,
the Goddess who grants all desires, and the Goddess who liberates from all suffering.
The goddess who pacifies all death, destroys all obstacles,
is beautiful in every limb, and bestows all prosperity.
In the *Jñānārṇava*: "One should worship the goddess Tripurāśrī, the bestower of all siddhis, who stands before the Mistress of the Wheel (cakranāyikā), the goddess who bestows all siddhis."
Having displayed the *sarvonmādana* mudrā and having made the offering,
one should worship the Yoginīs who are the essence of the *sarvarakṣākaraikaka* mantra.
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
O Śrī Maheśānī Tripurā, whose eyes roll from great intoxication, the corners of your eyes are slightly reddened, and you possess full, round, and firm breasts.
Possessing the brilliance of a thousand rising suns, adorned with divine ornaments,
she holds a book and a rosary, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with her [other] hands.
"Dadhāti sakalā" is stated in the Vāmakeśvaratantra.
Having placed the two hands facing each other, with the middle fingers meeting at the center and the ring fingers below them,
the two index fingers should be positioned outside the navel.
Then, the two thumbs are like staffs, positioned at the tips of the nails of the middle fingers;
this mudrā is named Unmādinī. Dakṣiṇāmūrti speaks of the sixth [mudrā]:
"In the wheel that effects all protection, adorned with the letters of the alphabet..."
One should worship the Yoginī Nigarbhā in reverse order, beginning from the west.
Resplendent with the luster of a thousand rising suns, adorned with pearl necklaces,
their eight hands hold the noose, the goad, the gesture of knowledge, and the gesture of granting boons.
The Goddess should worship these [deities], which bestow desired fruits;
she is omniscient, omnipotent, and the bestower of the fruit of all sovereignty.
The Goddess consists of all-knowledge, she is the destroyer of all diseases,
her very nature is the support of all, and likewise the remover of all sins.
The Goddess consists of all bliss, her very nature being the protection of all;
likewise, the Great Goddess bestows the fruits of all that is desired.

Thus ends the third wave in the Śrī Saubhāgyataraṅgiṇī composed by the venerable Mukunda.
Now follows the ritual application.
During the fourth watch of the night, the practitioner, having awakened, washed his hands and feet, put on two clean garments, and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),

should meditate upon his own Guru in the form of Brahmā within the *brahmarandhra*— appearing peaceful, highly gracious, and bearing the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*)— and, having prostrated, [proceed] from the *mūlādhāra*...

Having meditated upon the Root-Vidyā—which rises as far as the *brahmarandhra*, resembling the rising sun, and as subtle as a lotus fiber—one should pass the remainder of the night through worship, recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth. Then, at dawn, by the command of the feet of the Sovereign of the Three Worlds, the Goddess of the Lords, who is the consciousness of the three worlds, [one should perceive] like the venerable Void. Rising in the morning, you...

For the sake of my beloved, I shall follow the course of worldly existence. O Śrī Tripurā, Sovereign Goddess, as I follow this worldly course by your command, O Mother, may rivalry, contempt, strife, and fear never overcome me. I know what is Dharma, yet I have no inclination for it; I know what is Adharma, yet I have no aversion toward it.
[The ritual] ceases. "O Hṛṣīkeśa, dwelling within my heart, I shall do exactly as I am commanded by you.

Having thus received the Goddess's command, he goes outside, performs the *maitrī* (friendliness) and other [preliminary rites], and prepares a tooth-stick with the mantra: *klīṃ kāmadevāya sarvajanapriyāya namaḥ*. Now follows the bath; therein, first the Vedic [method].
Having performed the ritual bath and having cast three handfuls of water consecrated with the root mantra upon one's head,

one should recite the first *kūṭa* [of the mantra] and say "Svadhā to the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*)," likewise at the end of the second *kūṭa*, "Svadhā to the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*"),
and at the end of the third, "Svadhā to the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*"). Having thus sipped water and completed the libations for the ancestors and others, [one proceeds].

At the end of the root mantra, one should satisfy the Goddess three times with the words, "I satisfy Śrī Mahātripurasundarī. Then, having put on two unwashed garments for the twilight rite (sandhyā) and having performed ācamana as before, one should pour water from the right hand into the left hand and perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) upon one's own head three times with the root mantra using the water dripping from that [left hand] with the right hand.

Having taken the remaining water with the right hand and brought it near the tip of the nose, one should visualize through the flowing nostril a dark-colored figure situated in the left side of the abdomen, having the murder of a Brahmin for its head, the theft of gold for its hands, the drinking of liquor for its heart, various major sins for its limbs, and minor sins for its body hair.

Having visualized the personification of evil (pāpapuruṣa) as having arrived there, one should meditate upon that adamantine stone (vajraśilā) and cause [the evil] to fall upon it. Then, having offered the water of honor (argha) three times with the mantra: *hrāṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ śrīsūrya eṣa te 'rghaṃ svāhā*, [one should visualize the deity] wearing a crown fashioned from a mass of radiant jewels, possessing the immediate luster of molten gold.
Meditating on her holding a noose and a goad, and granting fearlessness and boons, one should recite the Gāyatrī as follows: "Aiṃ! We know Vāgīśvarī; Klīṃ!

We meditate upon Kāmeśvarī; Sauḥ! May that Śakti inspire us. Having thus recited the Gāyatrī according to one's capacity, with water in hand and revolving the root-vidyā at the heart, one should return home.
19a) Now, the worship (pūjā).

Having returned home, washed his hands and feet, and sat upon a clean seat, he should extract the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) according to the path described by the Guru: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ* [to] the *Śrīpādukā* of the Yoginīs of the entire *Prakaṭa*, *Gupta*, *Guptatara*, *Saṃpradāya*, *Kula*, *Kaula*, *Nigarbha*, *Rahasya-ati-rahasya*, and *Parāpara-rahasya*.

"I worship; obeisance. Having thus fully worshipped the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Therein, first is the ritual placement of the hands: *aṃ* on the two middle fingers; *āṃ* on the two ring fingers; *sauḥ* on the two little fingers; *āṃ* on the two index fingers and the two thumbs; and *sauḥ* on the palms and backs of the hands. Then follows the ritual placement of the seat: *hrīṃ klīṃ* on the two feet.

*Sauḥ*, salutation to the seat of the Self (*ātmasana*). On the two shanks: *haiṃ ha klīṃ hsauḥ*, salutation to the seat of the wheel (*cakrāsana*). On the two knees: *hlauṃ hasa klīṃ hsauḥ*, salutation to the seat of all mantras (*sarvamantrāsana*). At the *mūlādhāra*: *hrīṃ klīṃ vleṃ*, salutation to the central seat of accomplishment (*madhyasiddhāsana*). At the heart, with the index, middle, and ring fingers: *aiṃ*.

*Namaḥ* to the heart; *namaḥ*. With the middle and ring fingers on the head: *klīṃ namaḥ śirase svāhā*. On the crest-lock with the thumb: *sauḥ namaḥ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*. From the shoulders to the navel on the body with the ten [fingers]: *aiṃ namaḥ kavacāya huṃ*. On the two eyes and the forehead, directed toward the heart: *klīṃ*.
Homage to the Eye, *vauṣaṭ*. With the index and middle fingers toward the directions: *sauḥ* homage to the Weapon, *phaṭ*.

Now, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of Vaśinī and the others: On the head: *aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ vlūṃ*, salutation to the goddess of speech Vaśinī. On the forehead: *kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ klhrīṃ*, salutation to the goddess of speech Kāmeśvarī. Between the eyebrows: *caṃ chaṃ*... [and so forth].

jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ plīṃ, salutation to Modinī, the goddess of speech; at the throat: ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ plūṃ, salutation to Vimalā, the goddess of speech; at the heart: taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ hsrīṃ, salutation to Aruṇā, the goddess of speech; at the navel: paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ ha sa la va yūṃ.

Japinī, obeisance to the Goddess of Speech. At the *mūlādhāra*: Yaṃ Raṃ Laṃ Vaṃ Jhaṃ Maṃ Raṃ Yūṃ; obeisance to Sarveśvarī, the Goddess of Speech. From the *mūlādhāra* to the ankles: Śaṃ Ṣaṃ Saṃ Haṃ Kṣmrīṃ; obeisance to Kaulinī, the Goddess of Speech. Then one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*). Now follows the preparation of the *argha* water. To one's left...
Having fashioned a square maṇḍala and having placed the ritual vessel (śaṅkha) there for the practice,
one should fill it with pure water and worship the six limbs therein. Having thus established the general arghya,
one should fashion a square maṇḍala near it— containing a triangle, a circle, and a hexagon— using that water, and [place] in the center...

Having worshipped the combined and individual *kūṭas* in the order of the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, center, and [other] directions within the triangles and hexagons using the six-limbed mantras, one should place the conch-vessel there while contemplating it as having the form of fire, and worship it with: "Obeisance to the fire-mandala consisting of ten kalās."
19b) Yaṃ, homage to Dhūmrārcis; Raṃ, homage to Ūṣmā; Laṃ, homage to Jvalinī; Vaṃ, homage to Jvālinī; Śaṃ, homage to Visphuliṅginī; Ṣaṃ, homage to Suśrī; Saṃ, homage to Surūpā.

*Namaḥ*. *Haṃ*, obeisance to Kapilā; *Laṃ*, obeisance to Havyavāhanā; *Kṣaṃ*, obeisance to Kavyavāhanā. Having thus worshipped in a circular form, one should place the vessel there. Then, having worshipped with "Aṃ, obeisance to the solar orb consisting of twelve digits," one proceeds clockwise upon it.

In a circular form: *kaṃ bhaṃ* salutation to Tapinī; *khaṃ vaṃ* salutation to Tāpinī; *gaṃ phaṃ* salutation to Dhūmrā; *ghaṃ paṃ* salutation to Marīci; *ṅaṃ naṃ* salutation to Jvālinī; *caṃ dhaṃ* salutation to Ruci; *chaṃ daṃ* salutation to Suṣumṇā; *jaṃ thaṃ* salutation to Bhogadā.

*jhaṃ taṃ* salutation to Viśvā; *ñaṃ thaṃ* salutation to Vodhinī; *ṭaṃ ḍhaṃ* salutation to Dhāriṇī; *ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ* salutation to Kṣamā. Having thus worshipped the solar digits (*sūryakalāḥ*), one should draw a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, and a square as before, worship them in the same manner, and [offer] milk mixed with sugar.
Having worshipped with honey or pure water, [one should say]: "Oṃ, salutation to the lunar maṇḍala consisting of sixteen digits.
Having thus worshipped, as before: "AṂ, salutation to Amṛtā; ĀṂ, salutation to Mānadā;
IṂ, salutation to Pūṣā; ĪṂ, salutation to Tuṣṭi; UṂ, salutation to Puṣṭi; ŪṂ, salutation to Rati; ṚṂ..."

Salutation to Dhṛti. Ṛṃ, salutation to Śaśinī. Ḷṃ, salutation to Caṇḍikā. Ḹṃ, salutation to Kānti. Eṃ, salutation to Jyotsnā. Aiṃ, salutation to Śrī. Oṃ, salutation to Prīti. Auṃ, salutation to Aṅgadā. Aṃ, salutation to Pūrṇā. Aḥ, salutation to Pūrṇāmṛtā. Thus.

Having performed worship in the four directions starting from the east, one should worship as follows: *glūṃ* salutation to Gaganaratna (the Jewel of the Sky); *slūṃ* salutation to Svargaratna (the Jewel of Heaven);

*mlūṃ* salutation to Martyaratna (the Jewel of Mortals); *plūṃ* salutation to Pātālaratna (the Jewel of the Netherworld). In the center, *nlūṃ* salutation to Nagaratna (the Jewel of the City). Thus one should worship, as before, within the triangle, circle, and hexagon.

Having drawn a square *yantra*, one should contemplate the line from the west to the southeast of the triangle as consisting of the sixteen vowels, and the line from the southeast to the northeast as consisting of the sixteen consonants beginning with *ka*. Having contemplated *hasau* in the center, and having worshipped the complete and partial *kūṭas* along with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) as before, [one recites]: *oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ sohaṃ*.

"svāhā. Having thus worshipped, one should worship with these two mantras: "hasakṣamalavarayūṃ ānandabhairavāya vaṣaṭ" and "sahakṣamalavarayīṃ sudhādevyai vauṣaṭ. Then, having recited the root-vidyā seven times, one should present incense and a lamp, and display the nine mudrās beginning with *saṃkṣobha*.

Then, one should sprinkle oneself and the ritual implements with that water. Next, one should place the vessels for the *pādya*, *ācamanīya*, and *madhuparka* offerings to the north of that. Then, having meditated upon the Goddess as before within the *vaidava-cakra*, [one should recite]:
*hasauṃ hasaklīṃ hasauḥ namaḥ*.

20a) One should perform the invocation with the three-part mantra: "O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, come here! Then, one should display the mudrās: Saṃkṣobhaṇī, Drāvaṇī, Ākarṣaṇī, Vaśyā, Unmādanī, Mahāṅkuśā, Khecarī, Vīja, and Yoni.
One should display [the offering]. Then, with the thumb and ring finger, one should satisfy [the deity] with honey, ghee, and so forth, three times.

Then, at the end of the root mantra, saying "Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, this is your *argha*, svāhā," one should place upon the head of the Goddess fragrant paste (*gandha*), flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), barley, tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, *dūrvā* grass, and water. In the same way, for the foot-water (*pādya*), one says "namaḥ."

[I offer] *iyāmāka* grain, *dūrvā* grass, lotus, and water for the feet. *Jātī*, cloves, and *kaṅkola* with water for the *ācamanīya* (water for sipping), saying "Svadhā" for the mouth. In a bronze vessel, [I offer] ghee, curd, and honey for the *madhuparka* (honey-mixture), saying "Svadhā" for the mouth. Then, [I offer] the *ācamanīya* again with pure water alone. [I offer] the bath-water, saying "Namaḥ"; the garment, saying "Namaḥ"; and the ornaments.
One should offer incense with "Namaḥ" and flowers with "Namaḥ," using the *tarjanī* and thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*) while uttering "Vauṣaṭ.

One should offer incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*) with the word "Namaḥ. Then, having again displayed the mudrās, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) three times as before. Then, [one should place] the fifteen Nityā goddesses within the body from the square...

Alternatively, one may worship after visualizing an external fire-mandala. If it is a triangle, one should visualize the five primary vowels (Ā, Ī, Ū, E, AI) extending from the tip of the right-hand line toward the tips of the other corners; within those [vowels], one should worship with: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Eṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Oṃ Namaḥ Kāmeśvari Icchākāmaphalaprade Sarvasattvavaśaṅkari Sarvajagat*.
KṢOBHAKARI HŪM HŪM AIṂ HRĪṂ KLĪṂ VLŪṂ SAḤ SAUḤ KLĪṂ AIṂ, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the Nityā Kāmeśvarī; obeisance! || 1 ||

Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Āṃ Aiṃ! O Bhaga, O Bhuge, O Bhagini, O Bhagodari, O Bhagabhagamāle, O Bhagāvahe, O Bhagaguhye, O Bhagayoni, O Bhagini, O Pātini, O Sarvabhagavaśaṅkari, O Bhagarūpe, O Nityaklinne, O Bhagasvarūpe! Bring all the *bhagas* to me! O Varade, O Ete, O Surete, O Bhagaklinne, O Drāvake!
O Mayadrāvaya, O Amoghe! O Bhavichchekṣubhakṣa, cause fear to all beings! O Bhageśvarī!

Aiṃ Vlūṃ Jaṃ Vlūṃ Bheṃ Vlūṃ Mauṃ Vlūṃ Heṃ Vlūṃ Heṃ! O Klinne, bring all these vulvae (bhagas) into a state of peace! Strīṃ Hara Vleṃ Hrīṃ! I worship the Śrī-pādukā of the eternal Bhagamālinī; obeisance!
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Iṃ Hrīṃ! O eternally moist one, you who flow with intoxication, svāhā! I worship the sandals of the goddess Nityaklinnā Nityā; obeisance! || 3 ||
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Īṃ Hroṃ Troṃ Kroṃ Vroṃ Cchroṃ Jroṃ Hmauṃ Svāhā. I worship the sandals of the eternal Bheruṇḍā; obeisance! || 4 ||
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Uṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Vahnivāsinī; I worship the venerable sandals of the Nityā Vahnivāsinī, salutation! || 5 ||

Having visualized the five vowels beginning with *u* (u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, lṛ) from the southeast to the northeast upon the eastern line, [one should worship] within them: *hrīṃ śrīṃ uṃ oṃ hrīṃ phreṃ saḥ nityaklinne madadrave svāhā mahāvidyeśvarī nityā śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ || 1 ||*
20b) Hrīṃ Śrīr-ṛṃ Hrīṃ! Salutation to Śivadūtī; I worship the sandals of the eternal Śivadūtī, salutation! || 2 ||
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ṛṃ Oṃ Hrīṃ Hrūṃ Kheca-ccha-kṣa Strī Kṣeṃ Hrīṃ Phaṭ! I worship the sandals of the eternal Tvaritā; obeisance! || 3 ||

Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ḷ Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, I worship the venerable sandals of the eternal Kulasundarī; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ḷ Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Hasakalaraḍaiṃ Hasakalaraḍīṃ Hasakalaraḍauḥ Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Hsaṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Vlūṃ Saḥ, I worship the venerable sandals of Nityānityā.
Homage! || 5 ||
On the northern line, from the northeast corner to the southeast corner, one should visualize the five [syllables] beginning with *ai*. Within them, [one should worship]:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ eṃ oṃ hrīṃ phreṃ mrūṃ hrīṃ hroṃ nityamadadrave hūṃ hrauṃ*, "I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the Nityā Nīlapatākā; obeisance! (1)
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aiṃ Hasakhphreṃ, obeisance to Vijayā; I worship the sandals of the eternal Vijayā, obeisance. || 2 ||
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Oṃ Dhauṃ! Salutation to Sarvamaṅgalā; I worship the sandals of the eternal Śrī Sarvamaṅgalā, salutation! || 3 ||

Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Auṃ Oṃ! Salutations, O Blessed One, Jvālāmālinī, Goddess, Goddess who effects the destruction of all beings, O Jātavedasī! Blaze, blaze with flames, burn, burn! Hūṃ Hūṃ Raṃ Raṃ Raṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! I worship the sandals of the eternal Jvālāmālinī; salutations!
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kroṃ; I worship the venerable sandals of the eternal Vicitrā; obeisance! || 5 ||

Then, having visualized the *visarga* in the center, one should worship there with: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aḥ, at the end of the root-vidyā, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the eternal Śrī Mahātripurasundarī; *namaḥ*. Then, on the first lunar day (*pratipad*), one should again worship Kāmeśvarī in her own place three times; likewise on the second day and so forth.

One should worship each of the Nityās, beginning with Bhagamālinī and ending with Paurṇamāsī, [during the bright fortnight]. In the dark fortnight, one should worship each of the Nityās, beginning with Vicitrā and ending with Kāmeśvarī. When there is an increase in the lunar days (tithis), one should worship one [Nityā] on two days; when there is a decrease, one should worship two Nityās on a single day. Then, once again, the root...

Then one should worship the Goddess; in the space between the east and the center, one should worship Vimalā and Jayinī in the middle, and then, following the sequence of one's own guru’s instruction, worship the lineage of gurus known as the Divine Stream (divyaugha), the Siddha Stream (siddhaugha), and the Human Stream (mānavaugha) in three rows starting from the east.
At the end of the Human Stream, one should offer salutations: "Obeisance to the Parameṣṭhi Gurus."
Salutations to the supreme gurus! Salutations to one's own gurus! Thus one should worship the gurus in general. If their specific names are unknown, one should worship with:

*Aiṃ* salutations to the gurus; *Aiṃ* salutations to the sandals of the gurus; *Aiṃ* salutations to the supreme gurus. Then, in the center of the inner triangle, in the southeast corner: *Oṃ Aiṃ* salutation to the heart, *namaḥ*.
In the northeast: Oṃ klīṃ, obeisance; obeisance to the head. In the southwest: Oṃ sauḥ, obeisance; vaṣaṭ, obeisance to the crest-lock (śikhā).
In the northwest: Oṃ Ai& Namaḥ Kavacāya Namaḥ. In front of the Goddess: Oṃ Klī& Namaḥ Netratrayāya Namaḥ.
In the four directions starting from the east: Oṃ Sauḥ Namaḥ Astrāya Phaṭ Namaḥ.
Then, on the first line of the square, in the four directions starting from the east: Hrī& Śrī& Aṇimā Siddhi Śrīpādukām.

I worship; salutations! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the śrī-pādukā of the siddhi of *laghimā*; salutations! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the śrī-pādukā of the siddhi of *mahimā*; salutations! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the śrī-pādukā of the siddhi of *īśitva*; salutations! Thus one should worship in the right-hand direction of the door and so forth, starting from the southeast (*āgneya*).

In the corners and on the southern sides: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of the accomplishment of mastery (vaśitva-siddhi), obeisance! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of the accomplishment of irresistible will (prākāmya-siddhi), obeisance! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of the accomplishment of enjoyment (bhukti-siddhi), obeisance! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the śrīpādukā of the accomplishment of desire (icchāsiddhi).

I worship; salutations! Between Nairṛti and Varuṇa: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Prāptisiddhi; salutations! Between Indra and Īśāna: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Sarvakāmapradasiddhi; salutations! On the second line, starting from the east, [the eight...]

On the left side: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of the goddess Brāhmī; homage! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of the goddess Māheśvarī; homage! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of the goddess Aindrāṇī; homage! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of the goddess Kaumārī; homage!

Homage! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of the goddess Vaiṣṇavī; homage! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of the goddess Vārāhī; homage! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of the goddess Cāmuṇḍā; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the venerable sandals of the goddess Mahālakṣmī.
I worship; salutations! || 8 ||

Following this is the worship of the wheel (*cakra*). If it is to be endowed with superior fruit, then on the third line, in the directions starting from the east, one should say: *hrīṃ śrīṃ drāṃ sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī-śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ*.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Drīṃ; I worship the Śrīpādukā of the Drāviṇī Mudrā; obeisance! || 2 ||
Klīṃ, I worship the Śrīpādukā of the all-attracting mudrā; obeisance! || 3 ||
Vlūṃ! I worship the Śrīpādukā, the mudrā of universal subjugation; obeisance! || 4 ||
In the left portions of the corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya), I worship the Śrīpādukā of Sarvonmādinī; salutations! || 5 ||
Krauṃ! With the great goad mudrā, I worship the venerable sandals; obeisance! || 6 ||
Hasa Khaphreṃ, I worship the Śrīpādukā of Khecarī Mudrā; obeisance! || 7 ||
Hasauṃ; with seed-syllable and mudrā, I worship the Śrīpādukā, obeisance! || 8 ||
Between Nṛti and Varuṇa: Aiṃ, I worship the Śrīpādukā of the Yonimudrā; obeisance!
Between Indra and Īśāna: 2 Hasraiṃ Hasphrīṃ Hsrauṃ, I worship the Śrīpādukā of the Trikhaṇḍāmudrā.
21b) Having thus worshipped, one should worship in front of Aṇimā with: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aṃ Āṃ Sauḥ, I worship the Śrī-pādukā of Tripurā, the Mistress of the Cakra;
obeisance.* Having thus worshipped, one should display the Saṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā. These...

"May the manifest Yoginīs in the Trailokyamohana-cakra, together with their mudrās, siddhis, weapons, vehicles, and retinues, be worshipped with all ritual offerings. Thus one should present the worship. This is the first enclosure. On the sixteen petals, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aṃ... [etc.]
The eternal Kāmākarṣaṇī is Kalāśrī. || 1 ||
Āṃ: the eternal Kalāśrī, who attracts through the intellect. 2.
I am the eternal Kalāśrī, the attractor of ego. 3.
Īṃ! Nityā Kalāśrī, the attractor of sound. 4.
Uṃ, the eternal digit Śrī Sparśākarṣaṇī. 5.
Ūṃ, the eternal digit of fortune who attracts forms. 6.
Ṛ, Rasākarṣaṇī Nityākalāśrī. || 7 ||
Ṛ& is the eternal digit Śrī, the attractor of fragrance. 8.
Ḷ, Citrākarṣaṇī, the eternal digit Śrī. 9.
Ḷ& is the eternal Kalāśrī, who draws forth steadfastness. 10.
And E is the eternal Kalāśrī, the attractor of mindfulness. 11.
Aiṃ! The eternal one who attracts you both is Kalāśrī. 12.
Oṃ, the eternal one who draws forth the seed-syllables, Kalāśrī. 13.

"May it be accepted. Thus one should offer incense. At the end of the root-vidyā: "Oṃ! Having offered five oblations, one should offer six oblations with the six-limbed mantras ending in *svāhā*: *aiṃ namaḥ hṛdayāya svāhā* and *klīṃ namaḥ śirase svāhā*. Then, one should recite the root-vidyā as much as possible.
Oṃ! O you who guard the secret even beyond secrets, accept this recitation performed by us.
O Goddess, may success be mine through your grace, as you abide within me.

Having thus offered the recitation (*japa*) to the Goddess, one should offer praise: "O glorious Śrīkoṣa, whose heart consists of the five lion-thrones, you who are the fruit of the wish-fulfilling vine; O you whose hands flash with beautiful jewels, you who bring joy to the four bodies and reside within the treasury of the four lineages."
I bow to the eternal bliss, the supreme Brahman, for the attainment of happiness. || 2 ||

I bow to the Mother, who is the embodiment of Gaṇeśa, the planets, the lunar mansions, the Yoginīs, and the zodiac signs; she who consists of the mantra "Harīṃ" and is the very form of the sacred seats (pīṭhas).
23a) I bow to the Great Goddess, the Mother (Mātṛkā), the Supreme Sovereign,
who brings about the cessation of the turbulent and surging play of Time.

Even when a single word or syllable is mastered, a man prospers; [this work] has been composed by those who have fashioned [their own glory] like the sun, the moon, Kandarpa, Śaṅkara, Anara, and Viṣṇu.
I salute the Goddess Mahāśrī Siddhamātṛkā, the Sovereign of All, by whose syllables the three worlds are adorned with the moonlight of the moon. 4.
I shall describe that Siddhamātṛkā, by which this triple world— from the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) down to the wind— is strung together like beads upon an imperishable great thread.
That which is the eleventh seed-syllable, the support consisting of the three times,
is the world seen even today, from the cosmic egg down to the shell of the universe.
She whose body is composed of the letters beginning with 'a', 'ka', 'ca', 'ṭa', 'ta', and 'pa',
who is beautiful in her limbs— the head, arms, heart, back, hips, and feet.
I bow to that Great Goddess, who is the extraction of the syllable *tām*, the essence of essences, higher than the highest, and whose form is supreme bliss.
Even today, the gods do not know even slightly about her—
who she is, from where she comes, or by whom she was created— she who is so beautiful as to be a mere conception of form.
I bow to this supreme, auspicious Goddess, whose form consists of imperishable syllables that produce the syllable Kṣa, and who shines with the surging waves of the family's creative power.
One should salute the eight groups [of letters] according to their sequential order, in which the group of eight measures resides, and then salute the Mistress of the Eight Great Siddhas.
I bow to the venerable Tripurā, who dwells within the Śrīpīṭha known as Kāmapūrṇaja, and who is the treasury of the four commands. 12.
Thus, one should offer praise with these twelve verses spoken by Vāmeśvara.
O auspiciousness of all that is auspicious, O Śivā, accomplisher of all goals,
O refuge, O Tryambakā, O Gaurī, O Nārāyaṇī, salutations be to you!
Reciting this verse seven times, one should perform five prostrations with the mantras *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*. Then,

having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with perfumes upon a vessel made of gold or other materials, and having placed therein nine lamp-vessels fashioned from barley, wheat-flour, or similar substances, and having filled them with ghee and lit the lamps, [one recites] *hrīṃ śrīṃ*.

Having consecrated [the vessel] with "glū& mlū& plū& nlū& hrī& śrī&" for Ratneśvarī, having displayed the *cakramudrā*, and having worshipped it with the *vidyā*, one should rise, lift up that vessel, and [sprinkle it] from the head down to the feet while reciting the root *vidyā* at the end.
Oṃ! O Goddess who possesses the entire wheel, united with the Mistress of the Wheel, you who are the ninefold self!
O Goddess, accept this *ārātrika* for my spiritual accomplishment.

Reciting this mantra nine times, one should perform the *nīrājana* rite. Then, having seated the Goddess upon a seat to the right and sitting down oneself, one should fashion a mandala on one’s left consisting of a triangle within a circle, which is itself within a square.
Having worshipped it with "Aiṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the all-pervading mandala," [one proceeds to worship] the northeast, southeast, and southwest corners of the Śrīcakra.

Having drawn four mandalas in the intermediate directions starting from the northwest as before, one should worship them in sequence with the mantras: *vāṃ vaṭukāya namaḥ*, *yāṃ yoginībhyo namaḥ*, *kṣāṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ*, and *gāṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ*. Then, [one should touch] with the left thumb and ring finger.
23b) Come, come, O son of the Goddess, Vaṭukanātha, radiant with a mass of matted hair, three-eyed, flame-mouthed!
Destroy, destroy all obstacles! Accept, accept this offering together with all ritual services! Svāhā!

With the left thumb, middle finger, and ring finger in the shape of a vulva: *Oṃ*. Whether in the upper realm of Brahmāṇḍa, or in heaven, in the expanse of the sky, on the surface of the earth, in the void, in the netherworld (pātāla), or in the depths of water or wind—wherever they may be stationed;
or in the sacred fields (kṣetra), seats (pīṭha), and secondary seats (upapīṭha)—may the Goddesses, having been gratified by the offering of incense, lamps, and so forth, [be pleased].

May those who are worthy of worship by the Lord of Devas protect us, O auspicious one, according to the rite: *yāṃ yoginībhyaḥ svāhā sarvayoginīnāṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having formed the left fist with the index finger extended:
*kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣaiṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ*, O Guardian of the Site (*Kṣetrapāla*), [accept] this offering (*bali*) accompanied by incense, lamps, and other articles.

"Grasp, grasp, svāhā! Having formed a fist with the left hand and keeping the middle finger extended: "Gāṃ Gīṃ Gūṃ! Then follows the meditation on the *kāmakalā*: [one meditates on] the point (*bindu*) together with the hair, ears, and other limbs, the face, the two points, the four arms, and the circle of the breasts.
Having visualized the *yoni* as being endowed with two feet and so forth, one should visualize oneself in that same form.

Then, by means of the *khecarī-mudrā*, one should unite the Goddess within oneself, saying, "Forgive me. "Having constructed a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with auspicious characteristics in the northeast of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), [one should prepare] either a rim (*oṣṭha*) measuring one thumb-joint in height, or a mandala of sand."

In that regard, O Dear One, one should perform the outlining: first, one should draw three lines from west to east with their tips pointing toward the east; afterwards, one should draw three lines from south to north.
Then, O Goddess, one should cause the northern ends [of the lines] to be made with the Heart-mantra;
then, having performed the sprinkling, one should proceed with vermilion (sindūra).
O Lord, O Goddess, or O Beloved, [one may do so] with saffron, or with camphor powder,
or with turmeric powder, or with powdered grain.
O fair-faced one, one should draw a triangle, a hexagon, and an eight-petaled lotus;
having placed a flower in the center for Tripureśī.
Then, the purification of the vessels, such as the *sruva* ladle and others, should take place.

This is optionally combined with the statement from the *Nārada-pañcarātra*: "One should carefully scrape [the site] with a blade of darbha grass while reciting the King of Weapons (astra-mantra), following the heart-mantra. Alternatively, there is sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with water and kuśa grass while reciting the Vāgbhava-mantra.
One should sprinkle with water from *kuśa* grass using the tips of the hands turned upward, according to the *Sārasamuccaya*;

or one should sprinkle with the *vāgbhava* [syllable], according to the statement in the *Sautrāmaṇī Tantra*; or one should sprinkle with the tips of the hands turned upward, as prescribed by the *sūtra*.
There is an option regarding the lines, such as those with three triangles and so forth; alternatively, there is a circle with six corners, according to the *Prapañcasāra*.
This is because of the statement in the *Sāradātilaka* and because of the independent scriptural authority (*nirapekṣa-śruti*) of the *Yāmala* and *Pañcarātra*:
"O fair-faced one, having divided the fire-altar (*adhibhūta*), consciousness (*adhidaiva*), and the sacrificial grass (*adhivāsas*) into two;
and having divided the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) and the vessel for the oblation (*rūsthālī*) into two, O fair-faced one."
And one should place the vessel for clarified butter and the vessel for rice according to the specific division of the Yugas.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, one should place the *sruva* ladle, the *sruc* ladle, the *praṇītā* vessel, and likewise the *prokṣaṇī* vessel in pairs, with their openings facing downwards.
Then, having taken water in the vessel, one should sacrifice with the *prokṣaṇī*;
having performed the purification three times, one should sprinkle with that water.
All those vessels shall become purified;
then, having turned them face upward, one should consecrate them with the *vālaka* grass.
Holding two tips of *darbha* grass, each the length of a span, with the thumb and the ring finger, one should purify [the ghee] with the *astra-mantra*.
Regarding this purification of the ghee, it is said in the *Śāradātilaka*: "One should purify it with the mantra 'utpunīyāt' and 'āplava'.
O Dear One, having strewn *dūrvā* grass all around the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [one should proceed].
The spreading of *dūrvā* grass and *uttarāgra* grass is called the *paristaraṇa*.

Having taken the *sruva* ladle with the left hand, one should then wipe one's own face with the tip of a *darbha* blade, starting from the west and proceeding toward the east in all four directions— east and so forth— surrounding it sixteen times.
Having wiped it three times, one should then lower the hand downward.
Then, O Goddess, once he has sat down, one should recite the mantra as prescribed.
"Or else, O lady of excellent hips, they indeed become purifiers;
the sense is that [the purification] is for the purpose of consecrating [the vessel] from below the *sruva* spoon. 'As far as the mouth' means starting from the base of the handle."
Having recited the root mantra, one should write "Salutation to the Kuṇḍa.
Then, O Goddess, one should worship the Kuṇḍa with this mantra.
Having invoked Kāmeśvarī, conjoined with the semen of Kāma, into the center of the *kuṇḍa* and having worshipped her, he should bring the fire into her womb.
One should gaze upon the root-vidyā, the eye, and the weapon with the pair [of mantras];
then, having inscribed it with the weapon-mantra, one should thereafter place it within a casket.
One should rotate [the fire] three times around the pit, moving from left to right in sequence;
having extracted the fire from the casket, one should cast it out with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
O Goddess praised by heroes, having worshipped the portion for the flesh-eaters in the corner belonging to the Rākṣasas with the armor-mantra (kavaca), he knelt upon the ground.
Having established the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) and the fire within the center of the sacrificial pit,
one should worship the Fire-god with the mantra "mūrtaye namaḥ."
Situated in the center of the navel-mandala,
one should worship by unifying the fire of knowledge with the external fire, proceeding through the two nostrils of the channel in succession.
Having uttered the root-vidyā, one should also utter "Āṃ So'haṃ";
then, having uttered the fire-consciousness (vahni-caitanya) ending in the letter Ṅ, it should be joined with the heart-mantra (hṛn-mantra).
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should contemplate Kāmeśvarī within the womb using this mantra; one should then apply the six limbs [of protection] to the body with the fire-mantra.
Sahasrārcis, Svasti, Pūrṇa, Uttiṣṭha, Puruṣa,
Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara are thus proclaimed.
One should join those [mantras] ending in the dative case with the six limbs in the lotus and the moment;
the meaning is that one should thus perform the sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of infusion) within the body of Fire.
When the *tāra* has reached Vaiśvānara, [one should say]: "O Jātavedas, bring [the gods] here!
O Lohitākṣa, then accomplish all rites as they ought."
The mantra accompanied by the wife of Vahni should properly worship Vahni;
one should meditate upon Vahni as gold-colored, bearing a spear and a svastika.
Abounding in the splendor of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and adorned with excellent golden ornaments—
having thus worshipped him, O lotus-eyed one, [place the oblation] into his mouth.
One should contemplate a hexagon there and worship the seven tongues of fire. In the *Prapañcasāra*:
"The [syllables] of the fire, ending with the bindu and joined with the syllables from 'sa' to 'ya', [are used]."

By this, there is the letter *repha*. *Ira* is Vāyu; *arghī* is the letter *u*. Furthermore, the seven tongues—Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Bahurūpā, and Raktā—are of the *sāttvika* nature.

Likewise, in the *Vāyavi-saṃhitā*: "Soma, Śambhu, Rudra, Indra, Vahni, Māṃsāda, Varuṇa, Anila, and Gocara; Hiraṇya and the others are situated in the tongues of fire in sequence. In the center is the one called Bahurūpā. Thus, the middle tongue is three-crested and is named Bahurūpā; that is its crest.

Blazing on the right and supreme on the left; in the *Jñānārṇava*, it is said that one should worship the tongues [of fire] in sequence with their seed-syllables. One should worship the six limbs in the six corners, the Mothers in the eight corners, and the world-protectors upon the orb of the earth; then one should worship the mature Fire.
Having worshipped Brahmā with sacrificial fees on the right, one should dismiss Kāmeśī.
Having worshipped the fire according to the rules,
one should invoke the King of Wheels, accompanied by all its rays, into the mouth of that [fire] born from stone.
Then, having performed the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma), one should perform the fire-oblation for specific desires (kāmanā-homa).
The Mothers—beginning with Brahmāṇī—and the world-protectors: Indra, Agni, Yama, O Goddess, Rākṣasa, and likewise Varuṇa.
One should worship Vāyu, Kuvera, and Īśāna in order, starting from the east;
and one should worship Brahmā and Viṣṇu in order, above and below—thus it is stated by [the author] himself.

Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*): Having smeared the sacrificial ground with cow dung, one should fashion a well-characterized fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) on a sand altar (*vālukā-sthaṇḍila*), measuring one thumb-joint in depth. One should place three leaves of *dūrvā*, *agni* (barberry), and *kuśa* grass, along with dry fuel, incense, and other offering materials (*validravya*), upon the *kuśa* grass in pairs and facing downwards. having mentally visualized within the heart the seat known as Yoga.
Right there, in the midst of the earth, one should perform the worship:
namely, the cultivation of friendliness, the preparation of the body, bathing, and the act of cleaning the teeth.

just as worship with flowers and other offerings is performed in the external space.

On the eighth day, the sacrificer should always be one who observes the vow;

The practitioner who bows with devotion to the cry of Śivā, to Śivadūtī, the bestower of auspiciousness, has his desires held in the palm of his hand.
In the Nārada Pañcarātra: One’s own mantra should not be taught [to others], nor should it be spoken in public;
the scripture must always be kept secret and protected like one's own body.
One should undertake a pilgrimage with effort, and there, one should give gifts according to one's ability;
one should also engage in recitation, listening, and the study of the scriptures.
Once one's own mantra has been established, it should never be employed for the protection of others; nor should one practice it even in times of calamity.
O Sage, one should perform the Gāruḍa or Bhūtavāda rites out of fear, for one's own sake,
or through supreme compassion, specifically for those who are helpless and not in the presence of an assembly.
During circumambulation, when setting out on a journey, and especially when making offerings,
as well as at dawn and while traveling abroad, one should repeatedly recite one's own mantra.
Whether in a dream or in person, if a miracle that brings great joy should suddenly occur, it must not be told to anyone except the Guru. Likewise,
one should especially bestow [this] upon women who are endowed with devotion to their husbands.

One should never speak unpleasant words, nor laziness, nor especially lust and anger,
in the presence of one's teacher or before the sacred fire, without covering one's mouth.
One should not harbor pride on account of wealth, caste, or physical labor;
nor should one ever consume the property of a guru, even if it has been given by him.

one should not abandon non-duality, the worship of the deity, or the teacher and the sacred fire.

one should not step over his shadow, nor should one walk ahead of the guru.

he should not display his own power or attempt to gather disciples in the presence of the guru.

in the presence of the *praguru*, a wise person should never prostrate to his own *guru*.

one should not give the Guru’s command, nor should one speak using "you" and similar forms of address.
In the Devyāgama: "One should worship the seat, the bed, the garment, the ornament, the sandals,

He who daily worships the gods, sages, ancestors, guests, and the sacred fires with a mind focused on the beginning [of all things],
