In the Varāha Purāṇa: "On the ninth day, the goddess Gaurī should always be worshipped with meditative concentration;
she will become the bestower of boons upon all the world—of this there is no doubt."
On the ninth day, a man will indeed become an eater of five kinds of flour preparations, or a woman will become endowed with wealth; of this there is no doubt.
These [rites], however, should be understood as pertaining to both sides; this is the distinction according to the Śruti.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa it is said:
"On that day, one should worship Maheśvara and likewise the host of Mothers."
Or, O King, he obtains a single mother according to his desired wish.
The Mothers are those beginning with Brahmāṇī.

Regarding that, it is said: "O King, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, when the moon is in conjunction with the Kṛttikās, a man who worships the host of Mothers shall obtain all his desires."
Or, O King, one may obtain a single mother as desired, provided one honors her—this is the implied meaning. In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"He who worships Śivā on a Tuesday with auspicious dūrvā grass and unbroken rice grains..."
That practitioner as well shall constantly obtain his desired object.
Thus it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa, concerning Durgā:
"By worshipping [the goddess] named Rohiṇī on the third lunar day of Vaiśākha and by the gift of a water-pot, one is glorified in the world of Śiva."
In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"In the month of Mādhava, on the fifth day of the dark fortnight,
on a Thursday, when the moon is in Uttaraphalgunī and the sun is situated in Bharaṇī or the like."
Hara took the daughter of the mountain according to the rite for the marriage of a maiden;
therefore, one should perform special worship of the Goddess, a great festival, and so forth. In the Devīpurāṇa: "On the eighth day of Vaiśākha, one should indeed bathe with mango fruits."
Having bathed the deity oneself with māṃsī, vālaka, and kāri, [one should proceed].
One should perform the anointing with camphor and fruit-pastes, offer incense made of the five fragrant substances, and worship the Goddess with *ketakī* and *campaka* flowers.

The food offering should consist of sugar-cane juice, a maiden should provide the meal for the Brahmins, and likewise the practitioner himself should break his own fast; he should also give a sacrificial fee according to his capacity.
O Bhārgava, by this one obtains the merit of bathing at all sacred fords;
indeed, it is a bath for oneself with mango fruits and their juices.
The fruit is nutmeg (*jātīphala*). [This is] from the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa* concerning the goddess Aparājitā. (29a)
O King of kings, in the month of Vaiśākha, on the ninth day of both fortnights,
one who is devoted to fasting should worship Caṇḍikā with devotion.
Resembling a swan, a jasmine flower, or the moon, and equal to Dhruva in splendor,
he ascends an excellent celestial chariot and is honored in the world of the gods.
In the Brahmapurāṇa.
Since she was first worshipped on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha,
she should therefore be worshipped there by women for the increase of their good fortune.
And with various offerings, dances, songs, and artistic performances,
according to the Kālikā Purāṇa.
Having fasted on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha,
he [should worship] on the ninth day with sesame seeds, gems, barley-gruel, and sweetmeats.
One should worship with milk, curds, honey, wines, and flour-cakes,
as well as with the blood and flesh of various animals.
Then, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight, three handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds should be offered according to the Durgā-tantra mantra.
When this is done on the tenth day, whatever sin has been committed over ten lifetimes goes to destruction, and one is born with a long life.

The Durgātantra will be described [in the following]. In the Bhaviṣyottara: "One devoted to fasting should worship Umā with devotion on the ninth day, indeed under the name Brahmāṇī, she who possesses a white form."
O best of kings, having performed the ritual of the red [flower] in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
one should personally eat rice mixed with milk-porridge while maintaining silence.
One should also feed a maiden and Brāhmaṇa women according to one's capacity on the ninth day of both fortnights. In the Devīpurāṇa:
"And likewise on the eighth day of Āṣāḍha, one should bathe [the goddess] with water at night."
Having bathed herself, she should also anoint her with camphor and sandalwood paste.
Having bathed herself with water infused with turmeric (*haridrā*), she should also bathe the Goddess.
With incense, sandalwood, camphor, and *vālaka*, and with white *siddhu* (fermented rice water),
she should offer foods filled with sugar and auspicious drinks.
O Brahmin, he should cause the maiden to provide food for himself as well.
One should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability while reciting the hymn to Mahiṣaghnī;
a garland of lamps made with ghee indeed grants all desires.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "O King of kings, he who, devoted to fasting with piety on the ninth day of both fortnights in the month of Āṣāḍha, should observe eating only at night..."
One should worship with faith the Mother named Maitrī, who is Durgā,
seated upon Airāvata, auspicious, and possessing a white form.
He shall become an attendant of Indra, possessing a thousand Airāvatas.
In the Vāmana Purāṇa: "After Hari’s sleep, on the third lunar day, Kātyāyanī, the daughter of the mountain, likewise sleeps on the eighth."
The remainder [is as follows]. Having performed the special worship here, the bed should be offered. In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:

"O King of kings, he who in the month of Śrāvaṇa observes the practice of eating only at night (*naktabhojana*), subsisting on rice with milk and sugar-cane juice, being intent on the welfare of all beings..."
Devoted to fasting, O Hero, on the ninth day of both fortnights,
one should always worship Caṇḍikā by the name "Kumārī."
Having devoutly fashioned an image of silver that is formidable yet destructive of sins,
one should offer *karavīra* flowers along with perfumes such as agallochum and sandalwood.
One should worship with ten-ingredient incense and also with sweetmeats;
one should devoutly feed young maidens, women, and Brahmins according to one's capacity.
Restraining his speech, he should afterwards eat, having made an offering of bilva leaves;
thus, whoever worships the Noble Lady endowed with supreme faith.
One goes to the supreme abode where the god Guha resides.
Likewise, on the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janmāṣṭamī,
one should perform a great festival for the Blessed Lady just as I have done.
Likewise, O men, that which is the ninth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada—
That Nandā is celebrated as one of great merit and a destroyer of sins;
O son of Kuru, he who worships Durgā on that day according to the prescribed rites [attains his goal].
One obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, the fruit is ten-million-fold."
"I worship the Goddess"—this is the ellipsis. In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, for the sake of attaining prosperity, one should worship the Awakened Sustainer of the World with a garland of lamps."
O Hero, by worshipping Caṇḍikā according to the prescribed rite for four months, one obtains that same merit on the ninth day of the month of Kārtika. This Durgā is the sustainer of the world.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*: "O Hero, that ninth lunar day which occurs in the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa is proclaimed as the highly meritorious Sānandī."
The man who, having fasted for three nights, worships the Goddess there,
attains the merit of a horse sacrifice in this world and is glorified in the realm of Viṣṇu.
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vṛścika, which is known as Pāṣāṇa-caturdaśī,
one should worship the Goddess at night with offerings of stone-food."
By the word "stone" (pāṣāṇa), a lump having that shape is meant.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*: "The fourth lunar day is named Varadā; on that day, Gaurī is well-worshipped."
On the fifth lunar day, one should perform [the rite] that bestows incomparable good fortune; even Śrī herself bestows prosperity.

On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, according to the *Kālikā-purāṇa*: "When the sun is situated in the zodiac sign of Capricorn, it shall be the bright fifth; on that day, having duly worshipped Śivā with this mantra."
By means of this ten-syllable mantra of Jayadurgā; as stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa:

"Having worshipped the Goddess again according to the prescribed rite on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, one should perform the offerings of oblations (bali) and rites for the spirits (bhūtas) on the ninth day."
And at twilight, one should offer an oblation with the blood drawn from one's own body;
when this is done, one is joined with auspiciousness and rejoices eternally.
May he be blessed with abundance of sons and grandsons, with plenty of wealth and grain,
and may he be long-lived and endowed with all auspiciousness in this world.
In the *Smṛtisamuccaya*:
"When the sun is situated in Capricorn, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
Kālikā should be worshipped during that night for the pacification of all obstacles."
Having kept a vigil at night and worshipped the beloved of Hari,
one obtains one's desired objects, as well as a dear son and wealth.

30a) This [tithi] should be taken as that which extends through the time of Pradoṣa; when it extends through both [days], or does not extend through either, it must be the one joined with the preceding day (pūrvaviddha).
Likewise, the eighth day of the dark fortnight and the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight must be observed as joined with the preceding day.
"Parividdhā [is not valid] for anything whatsoever," according to the statement of Āpastamba. In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"He who avoids salt on the third lunar day beginning with Phālguna should, upon its completion, give a bed and a house together with attendants."
Having honored a Brahmin couple with the words, "May Bhavānī be pleased," one dwells in the world of Gaurī for a kalpa; this is called the Saubhāgya-vrata.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*: "On the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Umā should be worshipped by those seeking rewards. In the *Skandapurāṇa*:

Having reached the month of Vaiśākha during the spring season, a woman who desires her husband’s affection should perform a bath with sesame seeds on the third lunar day of the bright fortnight in the forenoon.
The goddess Pārvatī is indeed to be worshipped for the fulfillment of all desires.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"In the spring season, on the ninth lunar day, when it coincides with the Mṛga constellation, the goddess [is to be worshipped]."
She arose at midnight, like the Gaṅgā from the orb of the moon.
Therefore, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight, she should be especially worshipped here.
Now follows the offering of the *damanaka* flower.
In the *Jñānārṇava*: "I shall describe the planting of the *damanaka* for the benefit of practitioners,
O Dear One, so that the worship performed throughout the year may become complete."
O Mountain, whenever Damana becomes capable of breaking my asceticism,
then my wife Rati and Prīti shall be reduced to ashes, bringing me great sorrow.
From the tears produced from those eyes, the damana creeper arose;
its fragrance, O fair-eyed one, possessed great auspiciousness.
Pleased by that, O Goddess, a boon was granted by me in my heart, O beloved;
for the sake of Rati and Prīti, the Damana flower was manifested for them.
And for the practitioner who worships with *damanaka* flowers for the duration of a year,
his worship of Madana for that entire year shall be accomplished.
Thus, O goddess worshipped by the gods, it was by me alone that this [vow] was granted to him;
therefore, O goddess worshipped by heroes, the worship of Damana must indeed be performed.
Otherwise, that fruit becomes merely annual for the King of Desire (Kāmarāja).
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā it is said: "As for the months beginning with Caitra, which occur in the bright and dark fortnights, each preceding time among these is the most excellent of all."
On the eighth day, on the fourteenth day, or even on the full moon day.
One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) either during the first part of the night or immediately;
O Śiva, be present here, having arisen from your own grace.
"Having been severed from non-auspicious actions, you must be led [to the auspicious] by the command of Śiva.
Having thus addressed [the disciple], the wise one should worship Rati and Kāma there.

Having himself produced the *damana* plant together with its roots and sprouts, he consecrated it, saying "Śiva. Having produced it at the very dawn, as it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*: "On the fourteenth day, at the time of dawn, immediately after the daily worship..."
One should extract it with the Astra-mantra and smear it with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
One should worship the consecration with sandalwood paste, flowers, and other offerings;
then, having fashioned a nine-cornered figure of great luster with vermilion.
Having placed nine jars filled with gold, gems, and other precious substances,
or the preeminent teacher should install a single beautiful jar.
In the Vāyavī Saṃhitā:
"O Goddess of the Suras, one should properly wash the pitcher— whether it be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay— with the Astra mantra."
It is strewn with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), honored with blades of kuśa grass and sprouts of dūrvā,
its neck encircled by a white thread, and provided with a pair of new garments.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "Taking up water-pots provided with golden interiors,
along with bowls of barley and rice, and adorned with garments and ornaments..."
One should place the jars for the bath while reciting the mantra "ājighra";
likewise,
one should set down a flawless jar and worship it with the mantra "varuṇasya".
[This is done] with the mantra: "Thou art the support of Varuṇa.
Likewise, in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Covered with mango sprouts and provided with a pair of garments and fruits. In the absence [of these], even a single garment may be used, as it has been stated.
"One should wrap the jar with a cloth that is extremely fine, pure, and new, having the nature of the *māyā-tattva*. Thus it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*.
"O Goddess, O Beloved, one should place the *damana* herb, together with its roots, into the vessel."
One should perform the subduing in nine ways and worship immediately thereafter.
Then, O beautiful one, with the seed-syllable of Ānandeśvara, which is differentiated,
[one should worship] nine times with the seed-syllable of Ānandeśvara together with the *bindu*.
One should worship the ninefold differentiated subduer in due order;
thereafter, one should indeed consecrate that very person with the Aghora-vidyā.
One should perform protection with the Astra-mantra, and thereafter with the Kavaca-mantra;
then, having formed the Triśūla-mudrā, one should whirl it above the mantra.

The connection is as follows: one should worship that which is divided ninefold by the seed-syllable of Ānandeśvara—that is, by the seed-syllable of Ānandeśvara together with the *bindu*, divided in nine ways—according to the sequence beginning from the center. [One worships] the Aghora-vidyā, followed by Śiva and Candra, ending with Modana, conjoined with Vahni.
O Dear One, [the seed-syllable] Vāgbhava consists of Śakti, distinct from Bindu, Nāda, Kalā, and so forth;
likewise, O Goddess, the Kāmabīja is then joined with Śiva and Candra.

The syllable *pṛthvī* (la), ending with the seed-syllable of fire (*ra*) and enriched by the day (*ha*), is known as the Kāmarāja-bīja. Tripureśī is the Śakti-bīja, beginning with Śiva (*ha*) [and followed by *sa*].
It should be understood that the bindu is placed in the position of the visarga. Likewise:
having drawn a mandala on the right, adorned with saffron and other pigments.
Having drawn an Aśoka tree, one should draw a triangular mandala.
The *Saṃhitā* states that the mandala is "Sarvatobhadra," meaning it possesses auspicious lotuses on all sides.
In its center, O Dear One, one should worship Kāma, who is youthful, of reddish luster,
wearing red garments, and possessing a red countenance, [flanked] by his two consorts on the left and right.
For the sake of attaining success, one should worship Kāma— the lord of the five arrows, who wields a bow, who is richly endowed with Rati and Prīti, and who is accompanied by Vasanta.
Having written Vāgbhava, Bhuvaneśānī, Śrī, and Kāma with the triad [of Kāmas], and "Kāmāya namaḥ," this is the Vidyā consisting of the letters of Rudra.
Having uttered the three seeds of desire, one should pronounce the mantra of Māra;
then "Ratye Namaḥ," O fair-faced one, consists of eight syllables beginning with "Rati."

31a) One should speak of *prīti* (joy) in the place of *rati* (pleasure); the mantra of *prīti* consists of eight syllables. In the sequence of *rati* and *prīti*, [the couple] are fair and dark-complexioned, adorned with jewels.
Holding a lotus and betel in her hand, resplendent in red garments,
adorned with the royal ornaments of the Goddess, and graced by a garland of flowers.
Having meditated upon Kāma in the left and right [sides] immediately thereafter,
one should subsequently worship Vasanta situated in the midst of a kadamba forest.
Fair-complexioned, holding a jar filled with nectar in his left hand,
and bearing a collection of various flowers in his right hand.
Likewise, in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā: "Kāma, Bhasmaśarīra, Naṅga, Manmatha, Vasanta, he who has the same name as his [consort], Smara, and the wielder of the sugarcane bow."
Puṣpabāṇa and Tārā are proclaimed as ending with the heart-mantra;
these are to be worshipped by Kāma in the eight directions starting from the east.
Having properly worshipped Madana with flowers, perfumes, unbroken grains, and other offerings,
one should, with a serene mind, recite the Anaṅga-gāyatrī as well as the Śakti-mantra.
Having joined "jagatsarūpāyai" with "vidmahe," one should immediately thereafter say "dhīmahi" after joining it with "kāmadevāya."
O Anaṅga, may that be the Gāyatrī: "May that Anaṅga impel us.
Homage be to the one with flower-arrows, who brings joy to the world.
O Goddess, thereafter one should offer salutations with this mantra: "To Manmatha, the eye of the world, and to him who is dear to Rati and Prīti."
Then, with the *damana* plant in hand, one should perform the formal invitation to the Goddess:
"Oṃ, O Śivā, Queen of the Gods, you have been invited by me at this very moment."
That should be performed as follows: first, having requested the full attainment according to your command, one should satisfy Tripurā with this mantra.
Then, having worshipped the Goddess of the Gods with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and other offerings,
and having presented the food offering according to the rules, one should thereafter pray to Śrīvidyā.
The sixteen-syllable mantra of the Mother of the World, which bestows the fruits of all desired objects:
*Oṃ samastacakracakreśi sarvapuṣpāyudhādibhiḥ*.
"O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Lord of Desire, fulfill all my desires. With this, one should pray to the Goddess; thereafter, O Sovereign, [one prays] to Anaṅga.

One should perform the worship with *damanaka* flowers while reciting the armor-mantra (*varma*); by means of that very mantra, one should perform the great worship in the center, interspersed with flowers.
Having prepared an excellent food offering (naivedya) according to the prescribed rite that is captivating to the mind,
and having offered camphor and betel leaf, he should pray to the God of Love (Nanga).
Having given [the gift] to him, having paid homage, and having propitiated him,
one should then joyfully engage in water-sports together with the companions.
The meaning is that one should perform the subduing (*damanam*) with the *kavaca* mantra and worship with that;
subsequently, he explains what is called "Anaṅga" with the words "and Anaṅga."
One should perform the gift of food endowed with the six flavors;
and in this manner, one carries out the ritual procedure for the offering of *damanaka* flowers to the perfected ones (*siddhas*).
His annual worship shall be presided over by Śrīvidyā.
Also, in the Jñānārṇava:
"O Goddess, one should perform the offering of the *damanaka* flower according to this procedure."
O daughter of the mountain, his annual worship becomes fruitful.

31b) Now, as for the ritual applications (*prayoga*): in the months of Caitra, Vaiśākha, or Jyeṣṭha, on the eighth, fourteenth, or full moon day— or on the preceding day— at night, one should go to the vicinity of the *damanaka* plant, wash one's hands and feet, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and [take] *kuśa* grass.

Having taken sesame stalks and preceded by the recitation of *svasti*, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Oṃ, today [and so forth], I shall perform the rite of preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), which is a constituent part of the ritual for the offering of *damanaka* flowers. Then: "O you who have arisen from the grace of Śiva, be present here!"
Having completely severed yourself from what is not the work of Śiva, you should bow down to her who is known as Śivā.
Having thus addressed [the deity] and worshipped Kāma there together with Rati and Prīti, one should return home; this is the *adhivāsa* (preliminary consecration).
Then, in the morning, having performed his daily obligatory duties (*nityakṛtya*), he himself goes to the vicinity of the *damanaka* plant and recites:
*sauḥ namaḥ astrāya phaṭ*. With this, he uproots the *damanaka* along with its roots, and [sprinkles it] with water while reciting: *aiṃ namaḥ hṛdayāya*.
Saying "Namas," one should smear [the image] with sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and musk, and place it in some vessel.

Then, having had the benediction (svasti) recited: "Oṃ, today, in the month of Caitra, when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Pisces, on the fourteenth lunar day of the bright fortnight, in the land of Bhārata, I, [name], perform the worship of the year [Amuka-saṃvatsara]."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—"I shall perform the installation of the jar for the sake of success"—one should, with the mantra *oṃ sindūreṇa*, fashion a nine-cornered mandala and place either nine jars or a single jar upon a heap of grains. Then [recite]: *oṃ ājighra kalaśaṃ mahyātvā viśantvindavaḥ punarurjānivartasvasā naḥ*.
Having established [the vessel] with the mantra: "May wealth, rich in milk, flowing in a thousand streams from the udder, enter me again," and then with the mantra:
"Oṃ, you are the support of Varuṇa; you are the pillar of Varuṇa; you stand as the prop of Varuṇa;
you are the seat of Varuṇa’s truth; you are the dwelling-place of Varuṇa’s will; sit upon the dwelling-place of Varuṇa’s truth."

One should fill [the vessel] with pure water. Then, having divided the *damanaka* plant nine times with the mantra *ha sa kṣa ma la ra yūṃ*, one should place it upon the jar. Having placed it in one jar—or in some vessel—in the center and in the eight directions, one should place *haṃ namaḥ* in the center and *saṃ namaḥ*, *kṣaṃ namaḥ*, *maṃ* [and so on] in the eight directions starting from the east.

Having worshipped with "namaḥ laṃ," "namaḥ raṃ," "namaḥ yaṃ," and "namaḥ oṃ," and having consecrated [the deity] with the Aghora-Bhairavī Vidyā— namely, "hasakhaphreṃ," "hasaphrīṃ," and "hasauṃ"— one should protect [him] with "sauḥ namaḥ astrāya phaṭ" and form the trident mudrā (triśūla-mudrā) with the mantra "aiṃ namaḥ kavacāya huṃ."
One should wave the *damanaka* flower above [the disciple]. Then, having drawn the *Sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala on one's own right side,

with an *aśoka* tree in the center and a triangle within it, one should visualize the Spring (*Vasanta*)— desirous, of reddish hue, youthful, adorned with red garments and ornaments, and accompanied by Rati and Prīti on his left and right.
Having meditated upon the Lord Kāma, who holds a bow and five arrows, one should invoke him with the words: "O Blessed One Kāma, come here!
and [worship] with the eleven-syllable mantra: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ klīṃ klīṃ kāmāya namaḥ*.

Having worshipped with water for the feet and other offerings, one should meditate on Rati—fair-complexioned, adorned with jewels, holding betel in her hand, and dressed in red garments—and worship her on the left using the eight-syllable mantra: *klīṃ klīṃ klīṃ kreṃ ratyai namaḥ*.
Elsewhere, having meditated on Prīti, who is dark-complexioned and possesses the same form as before, one should worship her with the aforementioned mantra.

Having worshipped [him] in the west, one should meditate upon the fair-complexioned [Vasanta], who holds a jar of nectar with his left and right hands and stands in the midst of a grove of various flowering *kadamba* trees; then one should worship him with: *oṃ vasantāya namaḥ*. Thereafter, in the eight directions beginning with the east, one should worship with: *oṃ kāmāya namaḥ*, *oṃ bhasmaśarīrāya namaḥ*, *oṃ*...
Salutation to Anaṅga. Oṃ, salutation to Manmatha; Oṃ, salutation to Vasantasakha; Oṃ, salutation to Smara;
Oṃ, salutation to Ikṣudhanurdhara; Oṃ, salutation to Puṣpabāṇa—having thus worshipped these eight, [one should recite]:
"We know him whose nature is the universe; we meditate upon the god Kāmadeva; may that Anaṅga inspire us."

Having recited the *kāmagāyatrī* as much as one is able, one should prostrate with the following: "Oṃ, salutations to the one whose arrow is the flower, who causes the bliss of the world, to Manmatha, the eye of the universe, and to the beloved of Rati and Prīti. Then, holding the *damanaka* flower in hand: "O Śivā, O Goddess of Gods, you have been invited by me at this very moment; let that which is to be done be fulfilled according to what is available."

"Previously, by your command. Having thus addressed the Goddess, he should worship the *vītyātā* as described in the *Ghaṭapaṭa*. Then, having prayed: "Oṃ, O Sovereign of the entire wheel, O Mistress of the wheel! O Goddess, O Sovereign of Kāmeśvara, fulfill all my desires with all flowers, weapons, and other offerings," he should consecrate the *damanaka* herb with the mantra: "Aiṃ, obeisance to the armor, hūṃ."

With that other flower as well, one should worship the Goddess again. Then, having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) and betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*), and having prayed for one's desires, one should worship with the *damana* plant. Thereafter, having engaged in water-sports together with the practitioners (*sādhakas*), one should perform the concluding gift (*antadāna*). Now, regarding the investiture of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*), it is stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
If one does not perform the *pavitraka* rite during the past year,
the fruit of that [omission] is forcibly taken away by wicked beings.
O beloved, the month of Āṣāḍha is excellent, Śrāvaṇa is middling, and the month of Bhādrapada is inferior;
this applies to both the dark and light fortnights.
It is highly recommended during the bright fortnight, but if that is not possible, the other [the dark fortnight] may be used;
it should take place on the fourteenth, eighth, or full moon day.
Likewise, in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Goddess of the Gods, beginning from the sun in Gemini until the transit into Libra,
there is the great worship with the sacred threads (*pavitra*) of the exceedingly radiant [deities]."
On both fortnights, one should perform the *pavitrārohaṇa* on the fourth, eighth,
ninth, or fourteenth lunar day.
Likewise, in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
First is the darbha-grass thread, then the lotus-fiber thread;
thereafter the linen thread would be most meritorious, and after that the cotton thread.
32b) One should not have the sacred threads made from silk or by anyone else;
a maiden or a devoted wife should weave the thread.
A widow, whether of virtuous character or of ill character, must never cause [the garment] to be made;
nor that which is clean, torn, burnt, or enveloped in fivefold smoke.
One should carefully avoid using such thread in this purificatory rite;
likewise, one should avoid that which has been used for other purposes, mouse-droppings, liquor, blood, or anything else defiled.
One should carefully discard what is soiled or dyed blue and red.
As stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"With one hundred and eight threads, fashioned from nine strands..."
That which is the highest is indeed the most purifying; half of that is recorded as the middling.
Half of that [measurement] would be the smallest; thus the *pavitraka* may be of three kinds.
Having bathed with nine threads, one should purify the thread by tripling it—having tripled it according to the stated rule.
Likewise, in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*:
One should prepare the sacred thread (*pavitra*) with threads of the smallest, largest, or medium size;
that which is the smallest *pavitra* consists of twenty-seven strands.
Five hundred and four threads are declared to be the supreme medium [measure],
while one hundred and eight threads indeed constitute the highest [measure].
The nine threads are to be designated by the word *tantra*.
That which is the smallest purifier (*pavitra*) should reach the navel;
one should join it with twelve knots according to the measure of one's own body.
The middle [section] should be the measure of the thigh; there one should apply twenty-four knots, as well as the measurement of oneself.
O Bhairava, it is declared that even one who has merely been born is the supreme purifier;
in that [thread], one should apply thirty-six knots according to one's own measure.

The meaning is that the sacred thread (*pavitra*) is made to reach the navel of the Śrīmūrti; in its absence, it is made according to one's capacity or by the measure of one's own body. Furthermore, it is the thread by which the knots are formed.
Those endowed with the proper characteristics should be made using threads of a different color than that.
One should make a knot with seven windings on the little finger;
for the middle finger, one should make it with double that number, and likewise for the thumb with triple that number.
Likewise: one should perform the common purificatory rites with three threads— the middle thread for the guru, the equal thread for the fire, and the equal thread for oneself.
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
"O Dear One, one hundred and eight [recitations] is the superior; half of that is the middling;
and half of that again is the inferior, or else, O Dear One, according to one's capacity."
With the mantras recited while [the disciple] lies supine, one should cause the ten knots to be made;
it is said that for others as well, one should do so according to one's capacity, as far as possible.
"O Dear One, listen: that which was to be recited by me through the mouth of Tatpuruṣa with the mantras arising from the face turned upward— that is, the seed-syllables of Bāla—
was performed on the day prior to the day of the offering of the *pavitra*, as stated at the beginning of that [rite] by you, Śiva."
Or else, O Supreme Goddess, one may perform the consecration immediately at night,
following the daily worship, together with the initiates (samayins).
The daily worship is performed at its proper time.
Oṃkāra, Soma, Vahni, Brahmā, Nāga, Śikhidhvaja, Sūrya, and Sadāśiva—all these are deities; they are not non-gods (asurāḥ).
33a) According to the *Prayogasāra*: "All the gods," "the Viśvedevas," and "all the deities"—
with these [names], one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa on the three threads in the ritual manuals.
And Kriyā, Pauruṣī, Vīrā, and the fourth, Aparājitā.
Jayā, Vijayā, Muktijā, Sadāśivā,
Manonmanī as the ninth, and Sarvatāmukhī as the tenth.
The deities residing in the knots should be worshipped; one should honor them with the ritual services (upacāras)—the word "the Goddess" is understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
Or, having consecrated the purifiers (pavitra) with the root mantra, one should worship the Kalās within them.
O Goddess of gods, O beloved, one should likewise remember the sixteen Nityās and Śrīvidyā.

The procedure for the acceptance [of the invitation] has been declared; thereafter, the propitiation should take place with the root mantra. The word "and" (ca) indicates the inclusion of other mantras as well.
Thus it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
"The preceptor, having consecrated [the vessel] with the head-mantra (śiromantra) and thereafter with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra),
should then sprinkle and subsequently wash it with the weapon-mantra (śastramantra)."
And having obstructed [the disciple] with the Bhava-mantra, one should indeed cover his eyes with the armor-mantra (kavaca),
and [anoint them] with yellow pigment (rocanā), saffron (kuṅkuma), red sandalwood, and sandalwood.
The most excellent preceptor should cause it to be made variegated with red ochre and other pigments so that it is very beautiful; having sprinkled it with the root mantra, he should install it.
The preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) consists of sprinkling the sacred thread (*vidyā*) with the head-mantra (*śiromantra*) and other mantras, and pouring water while forming a fist-closure.
As stated in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*:
"Having thus consecrated the sacred threads on the preceding day..."
On the following day, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon the purificatory blades of grass (pavitra).
At every knot, the wise practitioner should personally perform the ritual placement of the mantra;
O Bhairava, one should recite the mantra over the rosary using the tip of the thumb.
One should deposit as many *vatu* syllables as there are syllables in the subsequent text;
by means of those mantras, one should employ it with the limb of the deity.
The meaning is that one should join it with the six-limbed mantras using divine limbs;
and having thus performed the placement (nyāsa) of all [limbs], [one places] the purifier (pavitraka) upon the sacrificial vessel.

Whichever mantra belongs to whichever [deity], and whatever its visualization, meditation, and so forth, as well as its worship— one should worship with that very [mantra] and with that state of being, exerting great effort.
With those same two mantras, one should place the *pavitraka* upon his head.
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"The Goddess, having established the jar and filled it with gold and other materials..."
Having invoked the Goddess and worshipped her, one should worship her with the root mantra.
Then, having worshipped the cakra,
the preceptor should begin the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārpaṇa) for Śrīvidyā and for the Guru by means of the Guru’s name.
One should give the *pavitra* to the preceptor, and immediately thereafter to all [others];
then one should offer the *pavitras* to the three types of gurus.
One should perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) for the lunar days (*tithi*), the eternal ones (*nityā*), the groups (*gaṇa*),
and those situated in the nine wheels (*navacakra*), as well as for the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśī*) and the nine bodies (*navakāya*).
O Goddess of gods, having worshipped each member of the host of rays with devotion,
one should then worship the *pavitraka* and satisfy the gurus, O beloved.
With golden ornaments, garments, and various collections of wealth,
one should thereafter wear that sacred [object] through his grace.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa (33b):
"With clarified butter one hundred and eight times, or likewise with sesame seeds at the beginning..."
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations to Mahādevī, the practitioner [should proceed].
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā.
Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation, one should afterwards burn the *pavitraka* in the fire;
having burned the *agni-pavitraka*,
[as stated] in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*.
When the Pavitrāropaṇa rite has been performed, one should present a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
such as gold, sesame seeds, a cow, a gem, or even a vegetable.
Thereafter, the practitioner should utter this mantra:
"Oṃ, with garlands of gems and coral, and with mandāra flowers and the like..."
O Supreme Goddess, this is the annual worship; it is not for a temporary dwelling.
Thereafter, one should dismiss the Goddess with the procedures previously mentioned.
Even if a wise man should feed the Brahmins according to the prescribed rule,
the worship performed throughout the year becomes complete at the end of that year.
A man may dwell in the house of a goddess for thousands of millions of eons;
even here, there shall be beauty of countenance, good fortune, and incomparable prosperity.
In the Jñānārṇava: "One should perform the worship of the Kumārī, and then [one] should worship the group of married women (suvāsinīs). The word "should worship" is the ellipsis. Dakṣiṇāmūrti says:
And for one who performs this merit, other acts of worship are fruitless.
Now, the ritual procedure:

The offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrārpaṇa*) should take place in the month of Āṣāḍha; if that is not possible, in Śrāvaṇa; if that is not possible, in Bhādra; or, if that is not possible, in Āśvina during the bright fortnight. If even that is not possible, it may be performed on the fourth, eighth, ninth, fourteenth, or full moon day of the dark fortnight as well.

The material for the cord (*sūtra*) should be one of the following: *darbha*, lotus fiber, linen, cotton, silk, or hemp; it must be uncut by a needle, unburnt, untarnished, unused, not gnawed by rats, and not defiled by impurities.
Having tripled the thread three times over, the best length is one hundred and eight units or half of that.

Having fashioned three purifiers (*pavitra*)— designated as medium and small— with knots numbering thirty-six, twenty-four, or twelve according to the number of threads, or with twenty-one, fourteen, or seven windings made with hair-mantras, reaching respectively to the knees, thighs, and navel of the deities; [one should place] the middle one...

The *pavitra* for the Guru and the Fire is equal [in size] to that [of the deity]; for oneself, it is equal to the youngest [finger]. Having prepared fifteen *pavitra*s for the eternal goddesses (*nityās*) and the nine mistresses of the wheels (*cakreśīs*) using three threads according to one's capacity, one should perform the consecration (*adhivāsa*).

Now, the ritual of consecration (*adhivāsa*). Having performed the daily obligatory rites on the previous day, the practitioner, together with the initiates, should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as before during the night. Having placed the sacred threads (*pavitra*) in a certain vessel, he should [recite] over its nine strands:
*Oṃ oṃkārāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Oṃkāra); *Oṃ somāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Soma); *Oṃ vahnaye namaḥ* (Salutation to Vahni); *Oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ* (Salutation to Brahmā).
Oṃ, homage to Nāga. Oṃ, homage to Śikhidhvaja.
Oṃ, homage to Sūrya. Oṃ, homage to Sadāśiva. Oṃ, homage to the Viśvedevas. Thus.

Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings: *oṃ* homage to Brahmā; *oṃ* homage to Viṣṇu; *oṃ* homage to Īśāna. One should worship these at the three threads when they have been formed by the triple-threading. Then, at the knots: *oṃ* homage to Kriyā;
*oṃ* homage to Pauruṣī; *oṃ* homage to Vīrā; *oṃ* homage to Aparājitā; *oṃ* homage to Jayā.

Salutation! Oṃ, salutation to Vijayā; Oṃ, salutation to Muktidā; Oṃ, salutation to Sadāśivā; Oṃ, salutation to Manonmanī; Oṃ, salutation to Sarvatomukhī. Having thus worshipped these ten deities, and having worshipped the Goddess with all ritual offerings according to the rules, one should worship the sixteen Nityās upon the purifiers and [then] Śrīvidyā.

One should place [the syllables]. Then, having consecrated [it] at the end of the root-mantra with "klīṃ namaḥ śirase svāhā," and having sprinkled [it] with "aiṃ namo hṛdayāya namaḥ," and having sprinkled [it] below with the fist-closure [mudrā] using "sauḥ namaḥ astrāya phaṭ," one should [use] "klīṃ namaḥ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ" with the *sannirodhana* mudrā.

Having performed the enclosure with "Varudhya Aiṃ Namaḥ Kavacāya Hūṃ" while making the *avaguṇṭhana* (veiling) mudrā, having colored [the object] with yellow pigment (*rocana*) and saffron (*kuṅkuma*), having sprinkled it again with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), and having covered it with a new cloth, one should install it. Then, having performed the daily rites (*nityakṛtya*) and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as before, [one should place] the sacred thread (*pavitra*) on the right...

Having placed the *māyā* [syllable] upon the middle [finger], one should perform the ritual placement of the mantras (*mantranyāsa*) at each knot with the tip of the right thumb; thereafter, one should place the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) there. Then, having placed the purifiers (*pavitra*) in the sacrificial vessel and having invoked the Goddess therein, one should worship her according to the prescribed rite.

Having placed the purifiers upon that head with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā), one should give a purifier to the Guru as well. Then, having given [offerings] to the three types of Gurus, to the Tithinityās, and to the Nine Cakreśīs, one should give them to the deities of the enclosures (āvaraṇadevatās).
Thereafter, with gold, garments, and so forth—as stated in the Varāha Purāṇa: "On the fourth lunar day, [one should worship] Gaṇeśa and Pārvatī."
"Especially"—the word "worship" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, concerning Umā: "One should worship her;
one obtains one's desire from her alone, there is no doubt. "In her"—that is, on the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*). In the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
"Then a man should worship the goddess Ekānaṃśā with tranquility."
One obtains the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled.
Then, on the eighth day, it is said in the Varāha Purāṇa:
"On the ninth day, the goddess Gaurī should always be worshipped with meditative concentration;
she will become the bestower of boons upon all the world—of this there is no doubt."
On the ninth [lunar day], a man who eats five kinds of flour-based foods will indeed become wealthy;
or a woman will likewise become endowed with riches— of this there is no doubt.

In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*, concerning the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇacaturdaśī*), it is stated: "O King, by worshipping Maheśvara and likewise the host of Mothers (*mātṛgaṇa*) on that day, or the Mother Ekāmbā, one obtains whatever desired object one seeks. This is especially so during both fortnights."

The lunar day (tithi) associated with it should be observed. Likewise, beginning with the verse "Kīrtikā," [it says]: "O King, by worshipping the host of Mothers, a man shall obtain all desires; O King, by worshipping even a single Mother, he obtains his desired wish. The remainder of the sense is that one should worship the host of Mothers. [This is stated] in the Kālikā Purāṇa.
The practitioner who constantly worships Śivā on an auspicious Tuesday with dūrvā grass and unbroken rice grains shall attain his desired wish.
On the eighth and the ninth [lunar days], worship should be performed for the sake of prosperity;
"even on the eighth day and so forth" also implies the sense of "constantly.
Likewise, it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa:

Having worshipped Durgā on the third lunar day of the month of Vaiśākha under the Rohiṇī asterism, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā by the gift of a water-pot. This refers to the third day of the bright fortnight. Likewise, it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
In the month of Mādhava, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight, on a Thursday,
when the moon was in Uttaraphālgunī, and while the two white [planets] were in Bharaṇī and so forth.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "On the eighth day of Vaiśākha, one should indeed bathe with mango fruits;
having bathed one's own deity with water containing māsi and bālaka."
One should perform the anointing with camphor and fruit-essences, offer incense made of the five fragrant substances, and worship the Goddess with *ketakī* and *campaka* flowers.
An offering of sugar and milk, feeding of maidens and Brahmins,
and likewise a sacrificial fee according to one's capacity, effect the purification of oneself.
O Bhārgava, by this one obtains the merit of bathing at all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Bathing oneself with the juice of mango fruits yields the fruit [of that rite]; so too does the *jātī* fruit for the Goddess Aparājitā. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
She was born previously on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha;
therefore, she should be worshipped there by women for the increase of their good fortune.
And with various offerings such as songs, dances, fruits, and so forth;
likewise, in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Having fasted on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha..."
On the ninth day, he [should worship] with excellent sesame seeds, barley-gruel, and sweetmeats.
One should worship with milk, clarified butter, honey, wines, and flour-cakes,
as well as with the blood and flesh of various animals.
Then, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight, three handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds should be offered using the mantra from the Durgā-tantra.
When this is done on the tenth day, whatever sin has been committed over ten lifetimes goes to destruction, and one is born with a long life.
The Durgā-tantra shall now be proclaimed:
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha or Śrāvaṇa,
one should perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa), which is supremely pleasing to the Goddess.
In the Devīpurāṇa:

Likewise, on the eighth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, having bathed oneself, one should bathe [the deity] with water from the night [pool]; one should then smear it with sandalwood paste. "Niśā" refers to turmeric; having bathed oneself with that same water, one should [worship] with incense, sandalwood, camphor, musk, white sugar, and sour gruel.
O Brahmin, one should cause the girl to eat foods mixed with sugar, as well as auspicious drinks,
and likewise provide food for oneself.
One should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability and recite the hymn to Mahiṣaghnī;
a garland of lamps made with ghee likewise bestows all desires.
In the Vāmana Purāṇa, it is stated that after Hari’s sleep, on the third lunar day, the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī) sleeps;
thus, there is a special ritual for the Goddess’s worship and her bed here.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "On the ninth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, for the sake of attaining prosperity,
one should worship the awakened Mother of the World with a garland of lamps."
O Hero, by worshipping Caṇḍikā according to the prescribed rite for four months,
one obtains that same fruit on the ninth day of the month of Kārttika alone.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vṛścika, which is known as Pāṣāṇa-caturdaśī, one should perform worship on that very day; likewise,
on the ninth day of the month of Bhādrapada, which is the Navamī.
Having worshipped Durgā there, one shall indeed obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
On the ninth day of the month of Āśvina, the fruit is ten-million-fold; "I worship the Goddess" is the understood remainder [of the verse]. In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"When one worships Gaurī with night-meals consisting of stone-like food"—the meaning is: with food in the form of stone-clods. In the *Smṛtisamuccaya*:
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight when the sun is situated in Capricorn,
Kālikā should first be worshipped there for the pacification of all obstacles.

Having kept a vigil at night, one obtains the beloved of Hara, as well as desired objects, dear sons, and wealth. This [lunar day] should be taken when it extends into the evening (pradoṣa); if it extends into both [days], or does not extend into either, the earlier [day] is superior.

"The eighth day of the dark fortnight and the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight must be observed as increased by the preceding [tithi] alone; they should never be joined with the following [tithi]. This is because of such statements from the *Āpastamba* [Smṛti]. Also, in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* (36a):
The fourth is named Varadā; on that day, Gaurī, when well-worshipped, bestows incomparable good fortune. On the fifth, Śrī makes Rati dear.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "When the sun is situated in the sign of Capricorn, there occurs the Sita-saptamī; on that day, one should duly worship Śivā with this mantra according to the prescribed rite."
Having worshipped the Goddess again according to the prescribed rite on the eighth day of the bright fortnight with this ten-syllable mantra to be recited hereafter,
one should perform abundant offerings of sacrificial food (bali) on the ninth day.
And at twilight, one should offer an oblation with substances produced from one's own body that are not loathsome;
when this is done, she is joined with auspiciousness and rejoices eternally.
Abounding in sons and grandsons, and with an abundance of wealth and grain,
he is born in this world long-lived and blessed with all good fortune.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"On the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Umā should be worshipped by those who offer fruits"— the word "should be performed" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Having reached the beginning of spring, on the third day of the bright fortnight, a woman dear to her husband should perform a bath with sesame seeds in the forenoon.
The goddess Pārvatī is indeed to be worshipped for the fulfillment of all desires.
